title: Towards Efficient Reasoning in LLM-Based Recommender Systems via Model Merging
prompt:
I've been mulling over how to merge a slow-thinking, reasoning-heavy recommender with a fast-thinking, direct-prediction recommender in a training-free way, so that the merged model can inherit some of the conciseness of the fast-thinking model without wrecking the reasoning that underlies its predictions. The core idea I'm developing, which I'm calling REAM (head-level, reasoning-grounded merge coefficients), is built around three questions: (1) which attention heads matter most to the reasoning underlying the final prediction, (2) how sensitive each head is to the fast-thinking update, and (3) how the update should be allocated across heads to improve conciseness while limiting degradation in reasoning and recommendation quality.

Concretely, I'm characterizing each head's importance to reasoning through two complementary signals. The first is retrieval criticality, which measures how frequently a head retrieves segment-relevant evidence throughout the reasoning trace, following a retrieval-head criterion where a token counts as retrieved only if the generated token matches the segment-relevant evidence region and the head's max attention lands on a matching position in that region. This is aggregated over a slow-thinking calibration set of 500 correctly predicted, well-formed prompt-trace pairs from the validation split, with stopword/punctuation steps excluded and successful retrievals TF-IDF weighted, yielding R_{\ell,h} per the equation R_{\ell,h} = (sum over x, s, t of \tau_x(w_t) g_{\ell,h,t}^{(s)}(x)) / (sum over x, s of |K^{(s)}(x)| + \delta), which I then map through a log-z-score-sigmoid transform \kappa_{\ell,h} = \sigma((\log(R_{\ell,h}+\delta)-\mu_R)/s_R) to get a bounded retrieval criticality weight. The second signal is decision faithfulness, capturing how strongly each head connects the final rating to the preceding reasoning, computed by partitioning the sequence before the rate step into prompt, analyze (user+item), and match regions, measuring attention mass m_{\ell,h}^r via the formula m_{\ell,h}^{r} = (1/|D_slow|) sum_x (1/|T_rate(x)|) sum_{t in T_rate(x)} sum_{\tau in \Omega_r(x,t)} Att_{\ell,h}^{(x)}[t,\tau], and then defining faith_{\ell,h} = m_{\ell,h}^{match} / (m_{\ell,h}^{match} + m_{\ell,h}^{analyze} + m_{\ell,h}^{prompt} + \delta). Under grouped-query attention, I assign shared K/V projections the max score among member query heads: \kappa_{\ell,g}^{K/V} = max_h \kappa_{\ell,h}, faith_{\ell,g}^{K/V} = max_h faith_{\ell,h}.

Separately, I'm estimating how safely each head's parameters can be modified via head-level update sensitivity, using the diagonal empirical Fisher of the slow-thinking model \theta_S weighted by the squared fast-thinking update. I compute a teacher-forced loss \ell_{\theta_S}(x) = -(1/|Y(x)|) sum_t log p_{\theta_S}(y_t | y_{<t}, prompt(x)), then the diagonal empirical Fisher F_j = (1/|D_slow|) sum_x (\partial \ell_{\theta_S}(x)/\partial \theta_S^{(j)})^2, partitioned by the structure of W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O (query heads for Q/O, GQA groups for K/V). The update sensitivity for a slice c is d_c = sum_{j in c} F_j (\Delta_{F,j})^2, averaged into d_{\ell,h}^{QO} = (d_{\ell,h}^{Q}+d_{\ell,h}^{O})/2 and d_{\ell,g}^{KV} = (d_{\ell,g}^{K}+d_{\ell,g}^{V})/2.

I then combine these into a perturbation weight s_b = exp(\gamma(\kappa_b+faith_b)) d_b for each unit b (either paired Q/O parameters of a query head or shared K/V parameters of a GQA group), and solve a constrained optimisation separately for the Q/O and K/V unit sets: max sum_b w_b \alpha_b subject to sum_b s_b \alpha_b^2 <= \varepsilon and 0 <= \alpha_b <= \bar{\alpha}, where w_b = ||\Delta_{F,b}||_F, and \varepsilon = \rho \bar{\alpha}^2 sum_b s_b. This yields a water-filling solution \alpha_b^\star = clip(w_b/(2\mu s_b), 0, \bar{\alpha}), with \alpha_b^\star = \bar{\alpha} when s_b=0. The merged model is then \theta^\star = \theta_S + sum_b \alpha_b^\star \Delta_{F,b}, with FFN layers assigned the mean Q/O coefficient per layer, \alpha_{\ell}^{\star,FFN} = H^{-1} sum_h \alpha_{\ell,h}^{\star,QO}, except that I exclude layers 30 to 35 from FFN merging by setting their coefficients to zero, since validation showed merging those final layers degrades the accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

My setup is merging RecZero (\theta_S), a slow-thinking reasoning recommender fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct for structured reasoning, with an adapted TALLRec model (\theta_F), a fast-thinking direct-prediction model fine-tuned from base Qwen2.5-3B-non-instruct (adapted so it's behaviourally distinct rather than retaining instruct-style reasoning behaviour). Both task vectors share Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct as the base \theta_B. This is a training-free merge, and I'm using a common calibration/hyperparameter/hardware configuration across REAM and all baselines, evaluating on Amazon Book, Amazon Music, and Yelp using the Reason4Rec rating-prediction splits, with each instance providing a user's historical ratings and reviews plus a target item and a 1-5 rating label. I report MAE and RMSE for rating accuracy and mean generated tokens per response (Tok) as a proxy for reasoning verbosity, where lower is better for all three metrics.

My baseline currently is just the unmerged RecZero (\theta_S) model on its own: on Amazon Book, MAE = 0.665, RMSE = 0.9331, Tok = 313.58; on Yelp, MAE = 0.7769, RMSE = 1.1054, Tok = 314.54; on Amazon Music, MAE = 0.5433, RMSE = 0.851, Tok = 344.28.

My question about this setup: after switching from RecZero ($\theta_S$) (my baseline above) to REAM (ours), predict the resulting value for each: Amazon Book MAE; Amazon Book RMSE; Amazon Book Tok; Yelp MAE; Yelp RMSE; Yelp Tok; Amazon Music MAE; Amazon Music RMSE; Amazon Music Tok.

title: Towards Efficient Reasoning in LLM-Based Recommender Systems via Model Merging
prompt:
I've been ideating on how to allocate merge coefficients in REAM when combining a slow-thinking RecZero model with a fast-thinking TALLRec model, both built on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct/Qwen2.5-3B-non-instruct as described in my setup, and specifically on the role of the Fisher-based update sensitivity signal, d. The idea is that around the trained slow-thinking solution, the loss surface may be flat along some parameter directions and sharp along others, so since the fast-thinking update modifies each head along a specific direction and magnitude, the risk of merging depends on the loss sensitivity along that particular update direction. Following Fisher-weighted merging, I estimate this using the diagonal empirical Fisher of the slow-thinking parameters theta_S, computed from the average teacher-forced loss over each calibration example's full generated response (averaging over the response length so longer responses don't dominate), then weight that Fisher estimate by the squared fast-thinking update to get a component-level risk measure I'm calling head-level update sensitivity, d_c = sum over j in c of F_j (Delta_{F,j})^2. Fisher entries are partitioned by the structure of the attention projection matrices W_Q, W_K, W_V, and W_O: W_Q and W_O are divided by query head, while W_K and W_V are divided by shared GQA group, and to match merge-coefficient granularity I average slice sensitivities as d_{l,h}^{QO} = (d_{l,h}^Q + d_{l,h}^O)/2 for query head (l,h), and d_{l,g}^{KV} = (d_{l,g}^K + d_{l,g}^V)/2 for GQA group (l,g). A larger d_c is meant to indicate loss sensitivity to that portion of the fast-thinking update, calling for more conservative merging of that component. My setup applies this within REAM's head-level merge coefficient allocation, merging RecZero (the slow-thinking model, fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct for structured reasoning) with an adapted TALLRec model (the fast-thinking model, fine-tuned from base Qwen2.5-3B-non-instruct to get a behaviourally distinct direct-prediction model), using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct as the shared base theta_B for both task vectors. I'm running this as an ablation of REAM's three allocation signals -- retrieval criticality kappa, decision faithfulness, and this Fisher update sensitivity d -- evaluated on the full Amazon Music and Yelp test sets. title: Towards Efficient Reasoning in LLM-Based Recommender Systems via Model Merging
prompt:
I've been brainstorming about how to move beyond correlational evidence when identifying which attention heads matter for retrieval during slow-thinking recommendation traces, and push toward a causal validation of the retrieval-criticality signal. The idea is to operationalize retrieval criticality by measuring how frequently each head retrieves segment-relevant evidence throughout the reasoning trace, following the retrieval-head criterion where a head counts as retrieving successfully at decoding step t of segment s only if (Cond.1) the generated token matches a token in the segment-relevant evidence region K^{(s)}(x), and (Cond.2) the head assigns its maximum attention to a position with a matching token in that region. This is aggregated over a slow-thinking calibration set D_slow of 500 correctly predicted, well-formed prompt-trace pairs, with stopword/punctuation steps excluded and successful retrievals TF-IDF-weighted to emphasize rare tokens, giving R_{\ell,h} = \frac{\sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{slow}}}\sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}}\sum_{t}\tau_x(w_t)\cdot g_{\ell,h,t}^{(s)}(x)}{\sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{slow}}}\sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}}|K^{(s)}(x)|+\delta}, where S = {USER, ITEM, MATCH}, g_{\ell,h,t}^{(s)}(x) indicates whether head (\ell,h) satisfies Cond.1-2 at step t, \tau_x(w_t) is the token's TF-IDF weight, |K^{(s)}(x)| is the evidence region's content-token count for segment s, and \delta prevents division by zero. Since R_{\ell,h} is unbounded and strongly right-skewed, I map it to a bounded weight via a log-z-score-sigmoid transform, \kappa_{\ell,h}=\sigma((\log(R_{\ell,h}+\delta)-\mu_R)/s_R), where \sigma is the logistic sigmoid and \mu_R, s_R are the mean and standard deviation of \log(R_{\ell,h}+\delta) across heads, so larger \kappa_{\ell,h} indicates greater retrieval criticality. To test whether the heads identified by \kappa (and, separately, by decision faithfulness) are causally important rather than merely correlated with performance, I mean-ablate the top 5% of heads under each signal and compare held-out NLL and JSD against size-matched random-head ablations. For the mean-ablation itself, for head (\ell,h) with output slice o_{\ell,h}(x,t) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h} at output-position token t of sample x, I precompute a reference mean activation over D_slow, \bar{o}_{\ell,h} = \frac{1}{\sum_{x} T_x} \sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}_\text{slow}} \sum_{t=1}^{T_x} o_{\ell,h}(x,t), and overwrite each ablated head's output with this constant at every evaluation position for every sample, which removes the head's input-dependent signal while preserving its average contribution to the residual stream (I avoid zero- or uniform-attention substitution since both collapse generation entirely). My setup evaluates on Amazon Book, Amazon Music, and Yelp using the Reason4Rec rating-prediction splits, where each instance provides a user's historical ratings and reviews plus a target item, with a 1-5 rating as the label. The slow-thinking model is RecZero, fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct for structured reasoning, and the fast-thinking model is an adapted TALLRec model, fine-tuned from the base Qwen2.5-3B-non-instruct to obtain a behaviourally distinct direct-prediction model, since an instruct-initialised model might retain substantial reasoning and instruction-following behaviour even when fine-tuned for direct rating prediction. Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct serves as the shared base for both task vectors. My baseline is the size-matched random-head ablation, averaged over three draws, and it gets the following held-out NLL increase over the unablated model: Amazon Music = 0.028NLL, Amazon Book = 0.114NLL, and Yelp = 0.046NLL. Under that same size-matched random-head ablation averaged over three draws, my baseline gets the following held-out JSD: Amazon Music = 0.036JSD, Amazon Book = 0.036JSD, and Yelp = 0.034JSD.

My question about this setup: after switching from Random-head ablation (size-matched, averaged over three draws) (my baseline above) to Retrieval-critical head ablation (top-5% κ-selected heads, mean-ablated), predict the resulting value for each: Amazon Music held-out NLL increase over the unablated model (in NLL); Amazon Book held-out NLL increase over the unablated model (in NLL); Yelp held-out NLL increase over the unablated model (in NLL); Amazon Music held-out JSD under head ablation (in JSD); Amazon Book held-out JSD under head ablation (in JSD); Yelp held-out JSD under head ablation (in JSD).

title: Evaluating Rational Contracting in Natural Language
prompt:
I've been brainstorming around a setup where I evaluate LLM agents acting in a Supplier role against rational, non-LLM baseline policies, specifically looking at how a Supplier fares against an RE counterparty. RE here is approximated as non-engagement -- i.e. the counterparty either doesn't pay or doesn't deliver anything at all, so it's effectively a fully adversarial, immediately-defecting counterparty. My setup uses ContractSim, where I evaluate contract execution on 180 synthetic contracts in a Catering setting, spanning five P_sat levels and six contingency variants. I use rational baselines (RC, RE, RCC) as counterparties to eliminate variance that might otherwise come from unpredictable LLM opponents, and I run the LLM agents (Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.6 Flash, and GPT-5.6-Sol) inside a Concordia scaffold. The scaffold builds a static role prompt from the concatenation of the role's Goal and Private Info fields, substitutes environment parameters before each run, and at each decision point appends a request generated from the current game state. Rather than reconstructing each prompt from a bounded observation buffer, the scaffold maintains an independent, append-only provider conversation per agent, appending each new observation once so it persists in history, which keeps a stable prompt prefix for provider prompt caching, while also recalling the five observations most relevant to the current request.

On the performance-metrics side, I track four classes: Utility (realized payoff, with a compliant variant that removes positive payoff from contract-violating periods), Regret (payoff shortfall relative to RCC play on the same history, again with a compliant variant comparing compliant utilities), Compliance (turn-level contract compliance rate, with conditional measuring the rate before any counterparty defection, exploited measuring the rate after counterparty defection, and tit-for-tat measuring the rate at which compliance/defection is met with the same response), and Defection (fraction of games with any contract violation, split into unilateral defection without experiencing defection first, and reciprocal defection after the counterparty defects first).

My current baseline, for the ContractSim synthetic performance-game with the Supplier role facing an RE counterparty, gives: Utility: RE = 0.0 mean, Compliant Utility: RE = 0.0 mean, (Ex-Post) Regret: RE = 0.0 mean, Compliant Regret: RE = 0.0 mean, Compliance Rate: RE = 0.0%, Exploited Rate: RE = 0.0%, TFT Rate: RE = 100.0%, Defection Rate: RE = 100.0%, and Reciprocal Defection: RE = 100.0%.

prompt:
I've been brainstorming about how to formulate the flow matching objective for PCFlow when applied to restoration tasks, specifically whether the flow should be conditioned or unconditional. My setup is PCFlow trained on each of four restoration tasks—super-resolution, denoising, inpainting, and colorization—using the latent consistency flow matching objective, and I'm comparing an unconditional flow formulation against a conditional one across these tasks, evaluating with FID and LPIPS in each case. My thinking here is framed from an optimal transport perspective: the unconditional formulation may restrict the transport trajectory to remain close to the degraded manifold, whereas the conditional formulation enables transport with a generative prior. I'm also considering that other work (PMRF) reports limited gains from conditional transport, which is part of why I wanted to test this directly in my own setup rather than assume the same holds here.

title: Flow Straight to Reality: Perceptually Consistent Flow Matching for Efficient Image Restoration
prompt:
I've been brainstorming about how the choice of perceptual network for the latent consistency/perceptual loss (LCPL) affects PCFlow training on super-resolution, specifically comparing an external perceptual network versus an internal one.

For the external perceptual network, I adopt E-LatentLPIPS as the perceptual objective. Given a predicted latent $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_1$ and the ground-truth latent $\mathbf{z}_1$, the perceptual distance is computed between the corresponding latent representations by applying differentiable augmentation and measuring feature discrepancies in a pretrained network:
\begin{equation}
L_{\text{external}}(\mathbf{z}_1, \hat{\mathbf{z}}_1) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}_0,\mathbf{z}_1,t,\mathcal{T}}\left[\left\|f_{\text{VGG}}\left(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{z}_1)\right) - f_{\text{VGG}}\left(\mathcal{T}(\hat{\mathbf{z}}_1)\right)\right\|^2\right],
\end{equation}
where $f_{\text{VGG}}$ represents a VGG network pretrained on ImageNet and BAPPS dataset, and $\mathcal{T}$ denotes random differentiable augmentations implemented in E-LatentLPIPS. I separately train VGGNet for $256 \times 256$ resolution for these experiments, since the publicly available pretrained model from E-LatentLPIPS is trained on $512 \times 512$ images.

As an alternative, I'm also considering an internal perceptual network to reduce dependency on external modules, since E-LatentLPIPS relies on an externally pretrained network and may require additional training for dataset-specific tasks. The idea is to define the internal perceptual objective using the model itself. Letting $\{\phi_l(\mathbf{z})\}_{l=1}^{L}$ denote intermediate decoder features extracted from latent feature $z$, the internal perceptual loss is defined as:
\begin{equation}
L_{\text{internal}}(\mathbf{z}_1, \hat{\mathbf{z}}_1) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}_0,\mathbf{z}_1,t}\left[w_l\sum_{l=1}^{L}\left\|\hat{\phi}_{l}(\mathbf{z}_1) - \hat{\phi}_{l}(\hat{\mathbf{z}}_1)\right\|^2\right],
\end{equation}
where $\hat{\phi}_l(\cdot)$ denotes per-channel normalized features and $\{w_l\}_{l=1}^{L}$ are weight values assigned to each feature layer. This formulation is similar to the LPL loss except that binary map masking is omitted for simplicity.

My setup is PCFlow trained on the super-resolution task, in the base configuration without gradient alignment applied, so I can compare the effect of external versus internal perceptual networks for perceptual supervision. The external network corresponds to my reimplementation of E-LatentLPIPS, while the internal network corresponds to using intermediate and final decoder features.

My current baseline results using the external perceptual network (E-LatentLPIPS) on the super-resolution task are: FID = 46.03, PSNR = 23.58 dB, SSIM = 0.6604, and LPIPS = 0.3223.

My question about this setup: after switching from External (E-LatentLPIPS) (my baseline above) to Internal (decoder features), predict the resulting value for each: Super-Resolution FID; Super-Resolution PSNR (in dB); Super-Resolution SSIM; Super-Resolution LPIPS.

prompt:
I've been brainstorming around the conflict-free gradient update scheme I built into PCFlow, where the structural transport objective (LCFM) and the perceptual guidance objective (LCPL) can produce conflicting gradients during training. My current default design treats LCPL as the steering signal that should be preserved, and when \langle g_{\mathrm{LCFM}}, g_{\mathrm{LCPL}} \rangle < 0, I remove only the conflicting component of the structural gradient g_{\mathrm{LCFM}} via an asymmetric orthogonal projection, following the update rule \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta(\tilde{g}_{\mathrm{LCFM}}(t) + \lambda_{\mathrm{LCPL}}(t)g_{\mathrm{LCPL}}(t)), with \tilde{g}_{\mathrm{LCFM}}(t) = g_{\mathrm{LCFM}}(t) - \mathbf{1}_{\{\left\langle g_{\mathrm{LCFM}}, g_{\mathrm{LCPL}} \right\rangle<0\}} \frac{\left\langle g_{\mathrm{LCFM}}, g_{\mathrm{LCPL}} \right\rangle}{\| g_{\mathrm{LCPL}} \|^2} \, g_{\mathrm{LCPL}}. The motivation is that LCPL steers the transport trajectory toward perceptually realistic regions of the target manifold, while LCFM provides the reconstruction-oriented structural updates, so I only let structural updates through when they don't interfere with the perceptual objective.

As an ablation, I'm now comparing this default (projecting the structural gradient, g_{\mathrm{LCFM}} \rightarrow \tilde g_{\mathrm{LCFM}}) against the alternative direction: projecting the perceptual gradient instead (g_{\mathrm{LCPL}} \rightarrow \tilde g_{\mathrm{LCPL}}). My setup keeps everything else fixed — PCFlow trained on each of four restoration tasks (super-resolution, denoising, inpainting, colorization) with conflict-free gradient alignment enabled — and I just swap which gradient gets projected onto the other.

For the perceptual-gradient-projection variant (g_{\mathrm{LCPL}} \rightarrow \tilde g_{\mathrm{LCPL}}), my baseline results across the four tasks are: Super-Resolution FID = 45.66, Super-Resolution LPIPS = 0.3317; Denoising FID = 45.42, Denoising LPIPS = 0.28; Inpainting FID = 45.53, Inpainting LPIPS = 0.2935; Colorization FID = 45.21, Colorization LPIPS = 0.3599.

title: Flow Straight to Reality: Perceptually Consistent Flow Matching for Efficient Image Restoration
prompt:
I've been brainstorming how to schedule the perceptual weight in my Latent Consistency Perceptual Loss (LCPL) rather than keeping it constant throughout training. For context, my overall setup combines flow consistency and perceptual consistency in the training objective: L_total(θ) = L_LCFM(θ) + λ_LCPL L_LCPL(θ), where λ_LCPL controls the strength of perceptual steering relative to the structural transport objective. The LCPL itself is defined as L_LCPL(θ) = E_{z_0,z_1,t}[L_percep(f_θ^i(z_t, t), f_θ^i(z_{t+Δt}, t+Δt))], with t ~ U(0, 1-Δt), and L_percep can be instantiated as either L_external or L_internal. This enforces perceptual similarity between adjacent trajectory predictions across neighboring timesteps in latent space. What I'm brainstorming now is making λ_LCPL a function of the diffusion timestep t rather than a fixed constant, motivated by the idea that early transport steps primarily require stable global alignment between degraded observations and the target distribution, where too much perceptual supervision might introduce optimization conflicts, whereas later transport steps closer to the true image manifold could benefit more from perceptual supervision to recover fine structures and realistic details. The specific linear warmup schedule I'm considering is λ_LCPL(t) = λ_min + I_{t≥t_min}(λ_max - λ_min)((t - t_min)/(1 - t_min)), which progressively shifts the trajectory towards the target manifold. For this schedule I set λ_min=0, λ_max=0.5, and t_min=0.5. My experimental setup trains PCFlow separately for four image restoration tasks: super-resolution, denoising, inpainting, and colorization. I'm comparing scheduling methods for λ_LCPL, including constant, linear, and linear warmup schedules, measuring FID and LPIPS for each task. My current baseline, using a constant schedule, gives: for super-resolution, FID = 46.18 and LPIPS = 0.33; for denoising, FID = 46.12 and LPIPS = 0.279; for inpainting, FID = 46.25 and LPIPS = 0.2918; and for colorization, FID = 45.78 and LPIPS = 0.3551.

My question about this setup: after switching from constant (my baseline above) to linear warmup, predict the resulting value for each: Super-Resolution FID; Super-Resolution LPIPS; Denoising FID; Denoising LPIPS; Inpainting FID; Inpainting LPIPS; Colorization FID; Colorization LPIPS.

My idea is to compare different scheduling methods for this coefficient, including constant, linear, and linear warmup schedules, since the role of perceptual supervision could plausibly differ depending on how close the transport trajectory is to the target image manifold at a given timestep. Early transport steps might primarily require stable global alignment between degraded observations and the target distribution, where too much perceptual supervision could introduce optimization conflicts, whereas later steps closer to the true image manifold might benefit more from perceptual supervision for recovering fine structures and details. That's the motivation behind trying out different schedules.

For the linear warmup schedule specifically, I set the perceptual objective coefficient to increase over timestep $t$ according to:

\lambda_{\mathrm{LCPL}}(t)=\lambda_{\min}+\mathbb{I}_{t \geq t_{\min}}(\lambda_{\max}-\lambda_{\min})\left(\frac{t-t_{\min}}{1-t_{\min}}\right),
\end{equation}

title: Retrieval-Corrected Conformal Prediction for Time Series
prompt:
I've been ideating on a retrieval-based correction mechanism for conformal prediction in time series, and I want to lay out the setup and where the baselines currently stand. The core idea is to split the interval construction into a retrieval stage and a correction stage. In the retrieval stage, each prediction context is encoded into a retrieval key z_t = psi_f(X_t, hat Y_t) before Y_t is observed, using whatever predictable forecaster features are available (input-window embedding, forecaster representation, point prediction features, exogenous variables, or their concatenation). Once a response at time i is observed, the key is appended to a knowledge base along with the realized one-sided residuals e_i^+ = (Y_i - hat Y_i)_+ and e_i^- = (hat Y_i - Y_i)_+, stored separately to allow different upper and lower tail behavior. Before time t, the knowledge base is K_{t-1} = {(z_i, e_i^+, e_i^-): i<t}, so the interval at time t only ever uses past residuals. Retrieval itself is done via KNN: N_K(t) = KNN_K(z_t, K_{t-1}, d), where d is instantiated as Euclidean distance, returning the K past indices closest to z_t. Retrieved residuals can be treated uniformly or weighted by distance, with weights w_i(t) = exp(-d(z_t,z_i)/tau) / sum_{j in N_K(t)} exp(-d(z_t,z_j)/tau) for i in N_K(t), where tau>0 controls concentration and uniform weights recover the hard top-K case. These weights define an empirical distribution used to compute local residual quantiles separately on each side: tilde R_t^+ = Q_{1-alpha/2}^{w_t}{e_i^+: i in N_K(t)} and tilde R_t^- = Q_{1-alpha/2}^{w_t}{e_i^-: i in N_K(t)}, giving the retrieved interval tilde C_t = [hat Y_t - tilde R_t^-, hat Y_t + tilde R_t^+]. Since this retrieved interval is locally adaptive but not calibration-certified (the retrieved set is finite and data-dependent, and quantiles can be unstable or biased when proximity in key space doesn't track future error behavior), I add a correction stage. For each calibration index j, once Y_j is revealed I compute B_j = max{ (Y_j - hat Y_j)_+ / tilde R_j^+, (hat Y_j - Y_j)_+ / tilde R_j^- }, a scalar nonconformity score normalized by the retrieved local scale rather than raw residual magnitude. Letting q = 1-alpha and q_n the finite-sample conformal quantile level, the correction is hat c = hat F_cal^{-1}(q_n) = Q_{1-alpha}({B_j : j in I_cal}), and the final interval is C_t^RCCP(hat c) = [hat Y_t - hat c * tilde R_t^-, hat Y_t + hat c * tilde R_t^+]. Values of hat c above one indicate the retrieved intervals tend to be too narrow on calibration data, while values below one indicate conservative retrieved intervals; direct retrieval corresponds to fixing this multiplier at one, whereas RCCP estimates it from the B_j distribution. For my setup, I'm comparing RCCP against split conformal prediction (SCP), online/adaptive methods EnbPI and SPCI, and localized methods NexCP, HopCPT, and ResCP. All methods use the same temporal partitions, frozen point forecasts, and random seeds, with hyperparameters selected on the calibration split when needed. I train a global LSTM forecaster on each dataset and evaluate at significance levels alpha=0.05 and alpha=0.15 (rather than the main alpha=0.1), averaging over multiple random seeds, to check whether behavior holds beyond the main setting. My baseline (SCP) results are as follows. At alpha=0.05: Air - Delta Cov 0.12 percentage points, PI-Width 89.99 avg interval length, Winkler 152.0, Time 36.41 seconds; Solar - Delta Cov 0.71 percentage points, PI-Width 57.72 avg interval length, Winkler 88.49, Time 90.22 seconds; Wind - Delta Cov 0.25 percentage points, PI-Width 86.26 avg interval length, Winkler 120.47, Time 0.73 seconds; Electricity - Delta Cov 3.33 percentage points, PI-Width 0.3 avg interval length, Winkler 0.32, Time 0.21 seconds. At alpha=0.15: Air - Delta Cov 0.07 percentage points, PI-Width 49.49 avg interval length, Winkler 93.42, Time 37.97 seconds; Solar - Delta Cov 2.02 percentage points, PI-Width 23.01 avg interval length, Winkler 48.69, Time 90.88 seconds; Wind - Delta Cov 0.16 percentage points, PI-Width 51.13 avg interval length, Winkler 83.04, Time 0.72 seconds; Electricity - Delta Cov 5.83 percentage points, PI-Width 0.17 avg interval length, Winkler 0.21, Time 0.19 seconds.

My question about this setup: after switching from SCP (my baseline above) to RCCP (Ours), predict the resulting value for each: Air (α=0.05) Delta Cov (in percentage points); Air (α=0.05) PI-Width (in avg interval length); Air (α=0.05) Winkler (in score); Air (α=0.05) Time (in seconds); Solar (α=0.05) Delta Cov (in percentage points); Solar (α=0.05) PI-Width (in avg interval length); Solar (α=0.05) Winkler (in score); Solar (α=0.05) Time (in seconds); Wind (α=0.05) Delta Cov (in percentage points); Wind (α=0.05) PI-Width (in avg interval length); Wind (α=0.05) Winkler (in score); Wind (α=0.05) Time (in seconds); Electricity (α=0.05) Delta Cov (in percentage points); Electricity (α=0.05) PI-Width (in avg interval length); Electricity (α=0.05) Winkler (in score); Electricity (α=0.05) Time (in seconds); Air (α=0.15) Delta Cov (in percentage points); Air (α=0.15) PI-Width (in avg interval length); Air (α=0.15) Winkler (in score); Air (α=0.15) Time (in seconds); Solar (α=0.15) Delta Cov (in percentage points); Solar (α=0.15) PI-Width (in avg interval length); Solar (α=0.15) Winkler (in score); Solar (α=0.15) Time (in seconds); Wind (α=0.15) Delta Cov (in percentage points); Wind (α=0.15) PI-Width (in avg interval length); Wind (α=0.15) Winkler (in score); Wind (α=0.15) Time (in seconds); Electricity (α=0.15) Delta Cov (in percentage points); Electricity (α=0.15) PI-Width (in avg interval length); Electricity (α=0.15) Winkler (in score); Electricity (α=0.15) Time (in seconds).

I've been brainstorming about how conformal prediction methods allocate interval width across different error regimes, specifically comparing RCCP (retrieval-corrected conformal prediction) against SCP as a baseline on top of a backbone time series forecaster. The idea behind RCCP is that after retrieval produces a local interval, a correction step calibrates the remaining error by normalizing residuals against the interval produced by retrieval, rather than calibrating raw residual magnitudes directly. This makes the correction depend on how well retrieval estimated the local scale, instead of discarding that local information and falling back to a global residual threshold. My baseline gets, for SCP, a width adaptivity ratio of 1.0 on Air and 1.0 on Solar.

prompt:
I've been working on a way to probe how much RCCP's calibration quality depends on the specific choice of retrieval key and distance metric, as opposed to the correction step itself. In RCCP, each prediction context is encoded into a retrieval key $z_t$ before $Y_t$ is observed, where $z_t=\psi_f(X_t,\widehat Y_t)$ and $\psi_f$ can be built from an input-window embedding, a forecaster representation, point prediction features, exogenous variables, or their concatenation. Once the response at time $i$ is observed, the key is appended together with the realized one-sided residuals $e_i^+=(Y_i-\widehat Y_i)_+$ and $e_i^-=(\widehat Y_i-Y_i)_+$, stored separately so upper and lower tail behavior can differ, giving a knowledge base $\mathcal K_{t-1}$. At query time, RCCP forms a local residual set by comparing the query $z_t$ against the stored keys using a retrieval distance $d(z_t,z_i)$, where smaller values mean closer contexts, and retrieves the $K$ nearest past indices via $\mathcal N_K(t)=\operatorname{KNN}_K(z_t,\mathcal K_{t-1},d)$ to localize calibration to relevant residuals. The default setup instantiates $d$ as Euclidean distance. What I've set up now is a variant that swaps this out for an embedding-based retrieval key combined with cosine distance instead, keeping the rest of the RCCP pipeline (the correction step) unchanged, so I can isolate the effect of retrieval key construction and metric choice separately from the correction mechanism. My setup applies this on top of both LSTM and Transformer backbone forecasters, evaluated on the Air and Solar datasets at a target miscoverage of alpha=0.1. My baseline results, with the original RCCP retrieval configuration, are: on Air with the LSTM backbone, coverage gap (ΔCov) is 0.43 and Winkler score is 92.44; on Air with the Transformer backbone, ΔCov is 0.2 and Winkler score is 92.51; on Solar with the LSTM backbone, ΔCov is 0.42 and Winkler score is 26.08; and on Solar with the Transformer backbone, ΔCov is 1.77 and Winkler score is 29.29.

title: Retrieval-Corrected Conformal Prediction for Time Series
prompt:
I've been working on a retrieval-based approach to conformal prediction for time series, which I'm calling Retrieval-Corrected Conformal Prediction (RCCP). The idea has two stages. First, a retrieval stage builds local residual evidence: each prediction context is encoded into a retrieval key z_t=\psi_f(X_t,\widehat Y_t) before Y_t is observed, and once Y_i is revealed, the key is stored together with the realized one-sided residuals e_i^+=(Y_i-\widehat Y_i)_+ and e_i^-=(\widehat Y_i-Y_i)_+, kept separate to allow different upper/lower tail behavior. Before time t, the knowledge base is \mathcal K_{t-1}=\{(z_i,e_i^+,e_i^-):i<t\}, so the interval at time t only uses past residuals. At query time, I compare z_t against the stored keys using a retrieval distance d(z_t,z_i), instantiated as Euclidean distance, and retrieve \mathcal N_K(t)=\operatorname{KNN}_K(z_t,\mathcal K_{t-1},d), the K nearest past indices. Retrieved residuals can be uniform or distance-weighted via w_i(t)=\frac{\exp(-d(z_t,z_i)/\tau)}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal N_K(t)}\exp(-d(z_t,z_j)/\tau)} for i\in\mathcal N_K(t), where \tau>0 controls concentration, and uniform weights recover the hard top-K case. These weights define an empirical distribution used to compute local residual quantiles separately on the upper and lower sides: \widetilde R_t^+=Q_{1-\alpha/2}^{w_t}\{e_i^+:i\in\mathcal N_K(t)\} and \widetilde R_t^-=Q_{1-\alpha/2}^{w_t}\{e_i^-:i\in\mathcal N_K(t)\}, which define the retrieved interval \widetilde C_t=[\widehat Y_t-\widetilde R_t^-,\widehat Y_t+\widetilde R_t^+]. Because this retrieved interval is finite and data-dependent and locality alone doesn't imply calibration, I don't use it directly as the final interval; instead I evaluate it on calibration data and correct its remaining error. For the correction step, rather than calibrating raw residual magnitudes, I calibrate residuals after normalizing by the interval retrieval produced. For each calibration index j\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{cal}}, the retrieved interval \widetilde C_j is computed before observing Y_j, and once Y_j is revealed I compute B_j=\max\left\{\frac{(Y_j-\widehat Y_j)_+}{\widetilde R_j^+},\frac{(\widehat Y_j-Y_j)_+}{\widetilde R_j^-}\right\}, a scalar nonconformity score for the asymmetric interval. Letting q=1-\alpha and q_n the finite-sample conformal quantile level, I estimate the correction \widehat c=\widehat F_{\mathrm{cal}}^{-1}(q_n)=Q_{1-\alpha}(\{B_j:j\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{cal}}\}), and the final interval is C_t^{\mathrm{RCCP}}(\widehat c)=[\widehat Y_t-\widehat c\,\widetilde R_t^-,\widehat Y_t+\widehat c\,\widetilde R_t^+]. Values of \widehat c above one indicate retrieved intervals tend to be too narrow on calibration data, below one indicates conservative retrieved intervals; direct retrieval corresponds to fixing this multiplier at one.

My setup evaluates conformal methods with LSTM and Transformer backbones. For each dataset, observations are chronologically split into training, calibration, and test periods with proportions 40%, 40%, and 20% respectively. I train one global forecaster per dataset on the training period and keep it fixed during calibration and testing. Calibration observations are used only for conformal calibration, and all conformal methods are evaluated on the same frozen forecasts. Both backbones use hidden dimension 128 and batch size 256, trained for 150 epochs with Adam using learning rate 10^{-3}. I compare against representative conformal baselines for time series: split conformal prediction (SCP), online/adaptive methods such as EnbPI and SPCI, and localized methods such as NexCP, HopCPT, and ResCP. All methods use the same temporal partitions, frozen point forecasts, and random seeds, with hyperparameters selected on the calibration split when needed. I evaluate at significance level alpha=0.1, with hyperparameter selection and results averaged over 5 seeds, for each of the LSTM and Transformer backbones separately. I report empirical coverage, signed coverage gap (\Delta_{\mathrm{Cov}}=100(\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}-(1-\alpha)), in percentage points, negative meaning undercoverage), PI-Width (average interval length), Winkler score (jointly assessing length and miscoverage), and Calibration Time (the post-forecasting time to calibrate each conformal method and construct test intervals, which for RCCP also includes serialization of retrieval keys for knowledge-base construction).

My baseline currently is the ResCP localized method, which gets: on Air with LSTM, ΔCov = -0.14 percentage points, PI-Width = 61.35, Winkler = 101.57, Time = 102.75 seconds; on Air with Transformer, ΔCov = -0.28 percentage points, PI-Width = 61.45, Winkler = 102.21, Time = 98.77 seconds; on Solar with LSTM, ΔCov = 1.14 percentage points, PI-Width = 20.1, Winkler = 38.9, Time = 323.09 seconds; on Solar with Transformer, ΔCov = 1.94 percentage points, PI-Width = 20.69, Winkler = 38.41, Time = 317.41 seconds; on Wind with LSTM, ΔCov = 1.56 percentage points, PI-Width = 63.36, Winkler = 89.75, Time = 4.05 seconds; on Wind with Transformer, ΔCov = 1.49 percentage points, PI-Width = 64.83, Winkler = 93.41, Time = 3.87 seconds; on Electricity with LSTM, ΔCov = 1.23 percentage points, PI-Width = 0.16, Winkler = 0.23, Time = 1.77 seconds; and on Electricity with Transformer, ΔCov = 1.96 percentage points, PI-Width = 0.2, Winkler = 0.29, Time = 1.87 seconds.

title: Iterative Erasure Count Is Not an Affine-Invariant Concept Dimension
prompt:
I've been brainstorming a preprocessing ablation for the dense Euclidean iterative erasure procedure that recomputes coordinatewise training mean and standard deviation after each dense map at κ∈{1,2,3,5,10,100,1000}. The idea is mapped-coordinate restandardization under increasing anisotropy: erasure is performed in restandardized mapped coordinates, edited features are then unstandardized and inverse-mapped before the common attacker, and I retain the pre- and post-standardization condition numbers along with all validation predictions.

My setup uses V-JEPA2 layer 21 frozen features on the 100DOH official validation split. The real-feature maps are fixed before evaluation. The primary dense family is $A_\kappa=Q D_\kappa Q^\top$, where $Q$ is a randomized signed-Hadamard basis and the 1,024 diagonal entries of $D_\kappa$ are log-spaced from $\kappa^{-1/2}$ to $\kappa^{1/2}$. Five fixed maps are used per condition. Every post-edit feature is inverse-mapped before attack, and all probes are fit in the original training-standardized coordinates with the intact validation-selected $C=.01$, which is neither reselected nor transported across maps. At rank ten, 2,000 paired group-bootstrap replicates resample the 193 validation source videos and compare the mean of the five fixed mapped trajectories with identity.

As part of the same ablation family, I also use a secondary family of 20 positive diagonal maps with randomly permuted log-spaced scales, where coordinatewise restandardization cancels that family algebraically, plus twenty Haar orthogonal maps as a solver sanity check, and unshrunk empirical covariance evaluated on five diagonal maps per condition with no floor or shrinkage.

For the underlying model setup, I freeze facebook/vjepa2-vitl-fpc64-256, mean-pool hidden tokens, and use the validation-selected layer 21 for 100DOH (feature dimension 1,024). All rank audits use deterministic LBFGS logistic probes.

My baseline, before applying the restandardization ablation across κ, is: 100DOH rank-ten AUROC at κ=1 (identity/orthogonal coordinates) = 0.599 AUROC, and the post-standardization condition number at κ=1 (identity/orthogonal coordinates) = 2.09 ratio.

My question about this setup: after switching from κ=1 (identity/orthogonal coordinates) (my baseline above) to κ=10 (anisotropic invertible coordinate map), predict the resulting value for each: 100DOH rank-ten AUROC (in AUROC).

title: Decomposition-Induced Context-Memory Conflict: When Fact-Checking Pipelines Contradict Their Own Source Text
prompt:
I've been brainstorming a decoding-time intervention to see whether DI-CC (decomposer-introduced context correction) can be suppressed without any retraining. The idea is to adapt context-aware decoding (CAD), which mitigates context-ignoring behavior at inference time by contrasting the output distribution conditioned on context against the same distribution without it, amplifying the model's attention to context. This is a training-free, decoding-time intervention only.

My setup builds on Phase 0's elicited pool of 191 entities, generated through a decomposition pipeline whose instruction explicitly invites the decomposer to check facts against its own knowledge and correct errors. This fact-checking instruction is a necessary condition for the whole setup, not a minor detail: an earlier attempt using a neutral instruction (no invitation to fact-check) on the same perturbed biography yielded zero DI-CC cases, since the decomposer faithfully reproduced the tampered year rather than overriding it. So every DI-CC instance in this data was elicited into existence, not merely observed, and the elicited condition is deliberately not representative of natural decomposition behavior — its purpose is solely to guarantee enough DI-CC instances exist to test H0 with adequate statistical power.

For the CAD adaptation itself, I retain the subject's name in both branches, since removing it entirely would also remove the subject's identity. I implement the contrastive decoding loop as a hand-written greedy decoding loop maintaining two parallel KV caches (one per branch), feeding the same sampled token back into both. I did not adopt the official CAD implementation's multi-process batch-file framework, since it targets a different (multi-GPU, multi-model) deployment setting than my single-GPU, resumable-stage-script pipeline — only the decoding formula itself was reused.

My baseline, without CAD, on Phase 0's elicited 191-entity pool gives a DI-CC rate of 4.16%.

My question about this setup: after switching from Standard decomposition decoding (no CAD) (my baseline above) to Context-aware decoding (CAD) adapted to decomposition, predict the resulting value for each: Phase 0 elicited 191-entity pool DI-CC rate (in %).

title: Retrieval-Augmented Vision Foundation Models for Robust Leukemia Cell Classification across Multiple Microscopy Datasets
prompt:
I've been brainstorming ways to extend my LoRA-adapted vision encoders with a retrieval-augmented classification (RAC) mechanism. The idea is to add a parallel retrieval branch alongside the image encoder: at inference time, this branch queries pre-encoded training images, retrieves the $k$ most similar embeddings by cosine similarity, and aggregates their labels into a similarity-weighted vote. This retrieved signal is then fused with the base classification output to produce one final classification.

My current setup for the base classifier is as follows. I use Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), where low-rank update matrices are injected into the encoder's attention projection layers while the pretrained weights remain frozen; the LoRA parameters and a linear classification head are trained jointly. LoRA is configured with rank $r=8$, scaling factor 16, and dropout 0.05. This gives 296,450 trainable parameters for DinoBloom, 295,938 for BiomedCLIP, and 443,394 for CLIP, a small fraction of the roughly 86 million parameters in each encoder. Training uses the AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of $1\times10^{-4}$, batch size 128, and class-weighted cross-entropy, for a fixed budget of three epochs with mixed-precision computation. Light augmentation (horizontal and vertical flips, mild color jitter) is applied during LoRA training. The same LoRA hyperparameters and training budget are applied uniformly across all three encoders (DinoBloom, BiomedCLIP, CLIP) and both stages, to keep comparisons fair, and the held-out datasets are never used during training or hyperparameter selection.

For this particular experiment, I'm looking at Stage 1, which is a binary classification task distinguishing leukemic from healthy single-cell images. The broader benchmark evaluates three encoders under four configurations on a held-out dataset (D5) of 260 single-cell images of leukemic and healthy cells, where the leukemic cells are all of the ALL subtype but are still counted simply as leukemic at this stage, since the purpose of Stage 1 is just to separate leukemic from healthy cells before subtyping happens in Stage 2. Here, I'm specifically evaluating on the ALL-IDB2 dataset, which contains a balanced set of leukemic and healthy single-cell images (130 and 130).

My current baseline results (LoRA, without RAC) on ALL-IDB2 are as follows. For DinoBloom: Accuracy = 0.9308, Recall = 0.9308, F1-score = 0.9307. For BiomedCLIP: Accuracy = 0.7962, Recall = 0.7962, F1-score = 0.7886. For CLIP: Accuracy = 0.9115, Recall = 0.9115, F1-score = 0.9112.

title: SkillLens: Visual Skill Cards for Retrieval-Augmented GUI Action Prediction and On-Policy Distillation
prompt:
I've been developing a way to give a frozen computer-using agent a form of reusable visual procedural memory, rather than touching any model weights. The idea is that prior interaction experience gets converted (via a Trace-to-VSC process) into Visual Skill Cards that pair a procedure with state cues and visual evidence. At each decision step, the system ranks these cards against the current instruction and interface state, expands only the selected high-resolution evidence, and conditions the frozen executor on that evidence plus the live observation to predict the next GUI action.

A key design point is that retrieval and expansion are separated: cards are ranked first, and only the selected cards' evidence is expanded, since irrelevant VSCs can distract the executor and loading all card evidence for a single step is unnecessary. The default path is a lightweight, context-aware, site-aware text-indexed selector. Formally, the retrieval query at step $t$ is $q_t=Q(x,h_t,c_t)$, where $Q$ deterministically serializes the task instruction $x$, recent interaction history $h_t$, and selector-visible interface metadata $c_t$. For each card $s_i$, $d_i$ concatenates its identifier, name, goal, keywords, and available metadata; $\mathrm{Tok}(\cdot)$ returns the resulting token multiset, $\operatorname{supp}(\cdot)$ returns its unique-token support, and $n(u;r)$ counts token $u$ in record $r$. The shared support and coarse score are defined as \begin{equation}\begin{aligned}\mathcal{U}_{t,i}&=\operatorname{supp}(\mathrm{Tok}(q_t))\cap\operatorname{supp}(\mathrm{Tok}(d_i)),\\ r_i^{(0)}(q_t)&=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}_{t,i}}\min\!\left(n(u;q_t),n(u;d_i)\right)+b_i(c_t),\end{aligned}\end{equation} where $b_i(c_t)$ is a deterministic prior derived only from visible metadata (such as site or operation compatibility), and is zero when such metadata is unavailable. Coarse retrieval then produces \begin{equation}\mathcal{C}_t=\operatorname{TopK}_{K_c}(\mathcal{L};r_i^{(0)}).\end{equation} The default web path reranks only these candidates, using a compact candidate record $d_i^{\mathrm{cand}}$ containing the card identifier, name, goal, keywords, and visual tags: \begin{equation}\begin{aligned}\mathcal{M}_{t,i}&=\operatorname{supp}(\mathrm{Tok}(q_t))\\&\quad\cap\operatorname{supp}(\mathrm{Tok}(d_i^{\mathrm{cand}})),\\ r_i^{(1)}(q_t)&=|\mathcal{M}_{t,i}|+0.1r_i^{(0)},\\ \widetilde{S}_t&=\operatorname{TopK}_{K_s}(\mathcal{C}_t;r_i^{(1)}),\\ \widehat{S}_t&=\operatorname{TopK}_{K_e}(\widetilde{S}_t;r_i^{(1)}),\\ S_t&=\{s_i\in\widehat{S}_t:\chi_i(c_t)=1\},\qquad E_t=\bigcup_{s_i\in S_t} e(s_i),\end{aligned}\end{equation} where $K_s$ is the selection budget, $K_e$ is the smaller expansion budget, $\chi_i(c_t)$ is an optional compatibility gate based only on visible metadata (defaulting to one), and $e(s_i)$ deterministically loads the bounded textual and visual evidence of card $s_i$. This closes the runtime path from the candidate set to the evidence actually consumed by the executor. A full-load strategy would pay \begin{equation}C_{\mathrm{full}} = \sum_{s_i\in\mathcal{L}} C(v_i),\end{equation} whereas this approach pays only the expansion cost for the selected evidence: \begin{equation}C_{\mathrm{lens}}(t)=C(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{C}_t)) + C(E_t).\end{equation} The board term is incurred only by board-based selector diagnostics and is zero for the default text-indexed selector. This cost expression captures the central design choice: retrieval decides where to look, and expansion controls how much visual evidence the executor sees.

My setup keeps the executor entirely frozen and changes only the runtime context, comparing No-skill against retrieved VSCs (with visual evidence expansion under the K_e/K_v budgets) across several frozen VLM executors: GPT-5.4-mini, GPT-4o, Gemini models, and Qwen3-VL-2B. I'm evaluating on Multimodal-Mind2Web (Step SR, Action F1, Element Acc.), WebLINX-BG (Overall, Intent Match, Element IoU), and OSWorld-G (Grounding Acc., bounding-box (BBox) Hit, Valid Output), with values reported as percentages.

My baseline (No-skill) results are: on Multimodal-Mind2Web, GPT-5.4-mini gets Step SR of 77.2% and Qwen3-VL-2B gets Step SR of 4.6%; on WebLINX-BG, GPT-5.4-mini gets Overall of 12.8% and Qwen3-VL-2B gets Overall of 14.1%; on OSWorld-G, GPT-5.4-mini gets Grounding Acc. of 45.0% and Qwen3-VL-2B gets Grounding Acc. of 28.5%.

title: Path Integral Value Matching for Linear Quadratic Stochastic Optimal Control
prompt:
I've been working on a value-based approach to stochastic optimal control that I'm calling Path Integral Value Matching (PI-VM). The core idea builds on the observation that the path integral representation of the optimal value function has a recursive structure: for any $0 < t < s$, \begin{equation}\exp\left( - V(X_t, t) \right) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}^0}\Bigg[ \exp\left( - V(X_s, s) \right) \exp\left(- \int_{t}^{s} f(X_r,r)\,\mathrm{d}r \right) \, \Bigg | \, \mathcal{F}_t \Bigg], \quad V(x, 1) = g(x),\end{equation} where $X_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the state of the uncontrolled stochastic process. This follows from the tower property of conditional expectation by decomposing the path integral into intervals $[t, s]$ and $[s, 1]$. The recursive structure suggests dynamic programming techniques can be adapted to solve for the value function iteratively, so I employ temporal-difference (TD) learning to approximate the recursive value dynamics, replacing high-variance long-horizon integration with stable short-term bootstrapping, and further integrate the Girsanov theorem with experience replay to enable off-policy training.

Concretely, my setup uses a Path Integral TD loss: for a state $x$ at time $t$, with a fixed lookahead horizon determined by $s = \min(1, t + M\Delta t)$, the loss is \begin{equation}\ell(\theta) = \left\| V_{\theta}(x,t) - \hat{V}_{\theta}(x, t, s) \right\|^2,\end{equation} where the target $\hat{V}_{\theta}$ is estimated via Monte Carlo approximation of the path integral using $N$ sample trajectories: \begin{equation}\hat{V}_{\theta}(x, t, s) = -\log \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^N \exp\left( - \hat{\mathcal{W}}(X^{(j)}_{[t,s]}) - \hat{\mathcal{G}}(X^{(j)}_{s}) \right),\end{equation} where each trajectory $X^{(j)}_{[t,s]}$ follows the uncontrolled path measure $\mathbb{P}^0_{[t,s]}$ initialized at $X_t^{(j)} = x$, and \begin{equation}\hat{\mathcal{W}}(X^{(j)}_{[t,s]}) = \int_{t}^{s} f(X^{(j)}_r, r) \, \mathrm{d}r, \quad \hat{\mathcal{G}}(X^{(j)}_{s}) = \begin{cases} V_{\theta}(X^{(j)}_s, s) & s < 1, \\ g(X^{(j)}_s) & s = 1. \end{cases}\end{equation} This is distinct from a continuous limit of classical Bellman equations, and also distinct from risk-sensitive RL Bellman equations, since in my formulation the log-sum-exp applies to the optimal value function rather than to the value function itself.

For the experiments, I'm benchmarking on five tasks adapted from prior work: Linear Ornstein Uhlenbeck, Quadratic Ornstein Uhlenbeck (easy), Quadratic Ornstein Uhlenbeck (hard), Gaussian Mixture Models, and Many Well. The first three are unimodal SOC control problems, and I'm currently focused on those. I compare against several policy-based baselines, including relative entropy (RE), cross entropy (CE), variance (VAR), log-variance (LVAR), adjoint matching (AM), stochastic optimal control matching (SOCM), and stochastic optimal control matching with adjoint loss (SOCM-A). For the first three experiments I strictly align training hyperparameters with those used for SOCM. Across all experiments I use a 6-layer fully-connected neural network with GELU activations and the Adam optimizer. Since the ground truth optimal control is analytically tractable for these tasks, I use the control $\mathcal{L}_2$ Error as the primary metric: $\mathcal{L}_2 (u,u^*) := \frac{1}{d}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}^{u^*}} \left[ \int_0^1 \|u^* - u\|^2 (X^{u^*}_s, s) \, \mathrm{d}s \right]$, noting that this comparison is particularly stringent for my method since I infer the control indirectly via the gradient of the value function ($u = - \sigma^T\nabla V$), whereas the policy-based baselines optimize the policy directly. All experiments run on a single NVIDIA RTX 4060 GPU, with results averaged over four independent runs with distinct random seeds, and I also track training/inference timing per method.

For the adjoint matching (AM) baseline on the unimodal tasks, my current baseline results are: on OU Linear, control L2 error is 0.0 and time is 41.0ms; on OU Quadratic (easy), control L2 error is 0.00028 and time is 21.0ms; on OU Quadratic (hard), control L2 error is 0.00674 and time is 21.0ms.

My question about this setup: after switching from AM (my baseline above) to PI-VM (Ours), predict the resulting value for each: OU Linear Control L2 error; OU Linear Time (in ms); OU Quadratic (easy) Control L2 error; OU Quadratic (easy) Time (in ms); OU Quadratic (hard) Control L2 error; OU Quadratic (hard) Time (in ms).

prompt:
I've been iterating on an explanation for why pythia-410m locks onto a single token as temperature drops, and I want to pin down whether this is really an attracting fixed point of the argmax map rather than some artifact of the autoregressive setup. The idea is that at low temperature the update is essentially deterministic, so the dynamics are governed by the map $x \mapsto \arg\max p_r$, and a map with a genuine fixed point, as opposed to one wandering across many endpoints, is what would make the ring settle onto a single token. title: Putting Registers to Work: Task Registers for Token Pruning in Vision Transformers
prompt:
I've been brainstorming about how the token pruning decision in TAP-F is actually driven, specifically whether the ranking score used for hard selection should come from the task register versus a purely attention-based selection signal. My setup builds on TAP-F, which is built on a frozen ViT-B backbone with task-specific adapters: one shared backbone is frozen and the remaining modules (register, head, rank-8 LoRA updates) are trained for 480,000 optimizer steps, with each step sampling one task uniformly and activating that task's register, head, and LoRA updates.

The pruning mechanism itself works as follows. At a pruning block, the implementation slices the fused query-key-value projection. It first computes the key projection for every candidate patch and the query projection for the active register. After hard selection, it gathers the retained keys and computes the remaining query and value projections only for the sequence that enters attention. The class token and register receive any projections not already computed. Non-pruning blocks keep the original fused projection path. This ordering reuses the candidate keys for matching and avoids computing patch queries, values, attention, or MLP activations for removed tokens.

For the selection criterion itself, TAP orders patch tokens by decreasing score and uses the ascending original patch index to resolve exact ties, which makes selection deterministic at inference while preserving the requested cardinality. Concretely, given ranking scores $q_i^{(l)}$, original indices $o_i$, and an integer removal count $R^{(l)}$: if $R^{(l)}=0$, all patches are returned in their current order; otherwise, candidate patches are sorted by decreasing $q_i^{(l)}$ and then by increasing $o_i$, the first $N_l-R^{(l)}$ candidates are retained and the remainder removed, and the retained candidates are restored to their original sequence order before gathering, with both retained and removed sets keeping their original indices. Each retained token keeps its original spatial index, which recovery and relative-position bias later reuse. During training, this uses $q_i^{(l)}=z_i^{(l)}$, while inference sets $q_i^{(l)}=f_i^{(l)}$ and introduces no perturbation.

This is being evaluated at a fixed keep rate of rho=0.5, and each ablation changes one component while fixing the backbone, adapters, token count, training budget, and seeds, so register-related controls are isolated from other factors.

My baseline, using the full TAP-F model at this keep rate, gets: ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy of 82.6%, ADE20K mIoU of 45.8%, and COCO box AP of 52.5%.

My question about this setup: after switching from TAP-F full (my baseline above) to Attention selection, predict the resulting value for each: ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy (in %); ADE20K mIoU (in %); COCO box AP (in %).

title: Putting Registers to Work: Task Registers for Token Pruning in Vision Transformers
prompt:
I've been brainstorming around a mechanism I'm calling dense feature recovery, used within a TAP-F setup, and wanted to lay out the exact design and the ablation I'm running against it.

The core idea: for each removed token, TAP selects a retained stand-in in the normalized concatenated multi-head key space. Let $\mathbf{k}_i^{(l)}$ denote the concatenation of the keys already computed for selection and let $\widetilde{\mathbf{k}}_i^{(l)}=\mathbf{k}_i^{(l)}/\max\{\|\mathbf{k}_i^{(l)}\|_2,\epsilon\}$ for a small $\epsilon>0$. The immediate pointer and offset are
\begin{align}
\pi(i)&=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{j\in\mathcal{S}^{(l)}}
\widetilde{\mathbf{k}}_i^{(l)\top}\widetilde{\mathbf{k}}_j^{(l)}, \\
\boldsymbol{\delta}_i&=\mathbf{x}^{(l)}_i-\mathbf{x}^{(l)}_{\pi(i)}.
\end{align}
If an earlier stand-in is removed at a later layer, its pointer extends the chain to a token that remains active. At a read point $l_{\mathrm{read}}\geq l$, following that chain yields $\pi^\ast(i)$. TAP reconstructs the removed position as
\begin{equation}
\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_i=\mathbf{x}^{(l_{\mathrm{read}})}_{\pi^\ast(i)}+
\alpha_t^{(l)}\boldsymbol{\delta}_i, \qquad
\alpha_t^{(l)}=\sigma(\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{r}^{(l)}_t+v).
\end{equation}
Here $\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $v\in\mathbb{R}$ form the scalar recovery readout. The endpoint carries the later semantic state of the surviving path. The stored offset preserves the difference observed when token $i$ left the encoder. All ViT blocks retain the same residual-stream dimension, so the early offset can serve as a correction in the shared channel coordinates at a later read point. This is an approximation, since the intervening blocks do not provide an explicit transport map. The learned scale limits the contribution of an offset when that approximation is unreliable. TAP does not add offsets created by intermediate stand-ins because they arise at different depths and are not directly additive.

Stand-in assignment is deterministic. An exact similarity tie is resolved by the smaller original patch index. The pointer and its index operations are treated as discrete and receive no gradient. Gradients still pass through the removed feature, the selected endpoint, the stored offset, and the recovery scale. The implementation computes $\alpha_t^{(l)}$ once at each pruning layer and stores the single value for all tokens removed there. It does not retain the full register state for recovery.

For the ablation, I'm changing this one component while fixing the backbone, adapters, token count, training budget, and seeds, in line with how I'm running the other controls: register controls separate task identity from feature adaptation because a shared initial register may still receive task-specific adapter features, allocation controls record every layer count and verify the exact-budget identity for each image, and recovery endpoint controls reuse the same retained sets and pointers. My setup is TAP-F, which freezes one shared backbone and trains the remaining modules for 480,000 optimizer steps. Each step samples one task uniformly, activates its register, head, and rank-8 LoRA updates, and performs one update with a shared AdamW optimizer. Inactive task modules receive no update on that step. This schedule gives each task about 160,000 updates, and the three data loaders cycle independently with their task-native augmentations. I train each TAP-F setting with five joint seeds; segmentation summaries use all five runs, while classification and detection use the prespecified three-run subset that matches their task-native comparisons. I record the sampler seed, optimization seed, and realized task counts for every run. TAP-F uses a base learning rate of $10^{-4}$, weight decay 0.05, 5,000 warm-up steps, and cosine decay over the joint run. The low-rank updates target the fused query-key-value projection, attention output projection, and both MLP linear maps in every block. All tasks update the shared allocation readout, while only segmentation and detection update the recovery readout.

I use ImageNet-1K for classification, ADE20K for semantic segmentation, and COCO for joint object detection and instance segmentation. Classification uses a linear head, segmentation uses a SegFormer MLP head, and detection uses ViTDet with Cascade Mask R-CNN. Detection and instance segmentation share one task register.

My current baseline, with dense feature recovery turned off, gets 42.4 mIoU on ADE20K and 50.3 box AP on COCO.

title: Putting Registers to Work: Task Registers for Token Pruning in Vision Transformers
prompt:
I've been brainstorming an ablation around how TAP is actually trained at the selection/allocation stage, specifically comparing the constrained straight-through (ST) gradient estimator against a simpler independent-sigmoid-with-rate-loss alternative.

The core issue is that the hard ranking used by the sparse forward pass is not differentiable. My constrained-ST setup retains the hard sequence length but supplies a soft gradient through a constrained mask. The feasible continuous target is $Q^{(l)}=\min\{\widetilde R^{(l)},C^{(l)}\}$ at a non-final pruning layer and $Q^{(l_M)}=B^{(l_M)}$ at the final one. During training, perturbed scores are $z_i^{(l)}=f_i^{(l)}+\gamma_i$, with $\gamma_i$ a standard Gumbel variable. The soft keep probabilities satisfy $s_i = \sigma\!\left(\frac{z_i-\theta}{\tau}\right)$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{N_l}s_i = N_l-Q^{(l)}$. For $0<Q^{(l)}<N_l$, the left side is continuous and strictly decreasing in $\theta$, with limits $N_l$ and zero, so this equation has a unique solution. I solve for $\theta$ in FP32 with 32 bisection steps, starting from the interval $[\min_i z_i-20\tau,\max_i z_i+20\tau]$, which for the sequence lengths used here places the endpoint residual below $10^{-5}$. When $Q^{(l)}=0$, every token is kept and the solve is skipped.

The implicit derivative has a closed form. Letting $a_i=s_i(1-s_i)$ and $A=\sum_i a_i$, holding $Q^{(l)}$ fixed gives $\frac{\partial\theta}{\partial z_j}=\frac{a_j}{A}$ and $\frac{\partial s_i}{\partial z_j}=\frac{a_i}{\tau}\left(\mathbb{I}[i=j]-\frac{a_j}{A}\right)$. When the allocation readout changes $Q^{(l)}$, the additional derivative is $\frac{\partial\theta}{\partial Q^{(l)}}=\frac{\tau}{A}$ and $\frac{\partial s_i}{\partial Q^{(l)}}=-\frac{a_i}{A}$. These are exact for $A>0$; in implementation every denominator $A$ is replaced by $A_\epsilon=\max(A,10^{-6})$ to avoid numerical amplification after sigmoid saturation. Gradients pass through $Q^{(l)}$ while $\widetilde R^{(l)}<C^{(l)}$ and stop at the capacity bound, using a zero subgradient at equality. The integer budget passed to the next layer is detached, so each allocation receives a local gradient and the final layer consumes the remaining hard budget. The negative sign in the $Q^{(l)}$ derivative reflects the cardinality constraint: a larger removal target lowers total soft keep mass.

The hard mask keeps the $N_l-R^{(l)}$ highest perturbed scores, with a straight-through mask $m_i=\operatorname{stopgrad}(m_{i,\mathrm{hard}}-s_i)+s_i$: forward value binary, derivative following the constrained soft mask. Gathering the hard retained set after multiplying by $m_i$ keeps the actual encoder sparse, while also letting the scoring and allocation readouts receive gradients through the retained features; dense-task losses provide a second route through reconstructed removed features. The temperature follows a cosine schedule from $1.0$ to $0.1$. Gumbel perturbations are sampled only during training; inference ranks the unperturbed scores and is deterministic. The exact hard count removes the need for an auxiliary rate loss.

My comparison setup uses the constrained-ST variants and a hard-only control with the same initialization and sparse forward path — they differ only in the gradient estimator or its temperature. In the hard-only control, discrete decisions block the task-loss gradient to the scoring and allocation readouts. The independent-sigmoid baseline instead thresholds separate gates and controls their mean with a rate penalty, so its per-image sequence length may vary; every row reports its realized final token count alongside task performance. This setup is meant to separate the exact inference budget from the mechanism used to train selection and allocation.

For TAP training at keep rate rho=0.5, with the same initialization and sparse forward path, my baseline with constrained ST and cosine τ gets: ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy 82.6%, ADE20K mIoU 45.8%, and COCO box AP 52.5 AP.

My question about this setup: after switching from Constrained ST, cosine τ (my baseline above) to Independent sigmoid and rate loss, predict the resulting value for each: ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy (in %); ADE20K mIoU (in %); COCO box AP (in AP).

title: AI Research Preference Models
prompt:
I've been thinking about where the compute of an AI research agent actually goes. Proposing or modifying candidate code is quick, but executing a candidate to train a model and measure it can take hours, so an agent can propose far more candidates than it can afford to run, and the lever on progress becomes which candidates it chooses to spend GPU time on. Language models forecast absolute metrics unreliably in my early tests, so I frame the allocation as a preference-ranking problem instead: rank the candidate solutions and execute only the most promising one. The intervention is an Inference-only Research Preference Model (RPM). At each child-creation step the chosen parent node is mutated 15 times independently in parallel to yield 15 unexecuted candidate solutions, and the RPM selects the single candidate to execute through pairwise comparisons in a tournament knockout. Each comparison is a frozen Qwen3.6-27B judge reasoning over the two candidates' plans and code together with context from the search so far: up to K non-buggy previously evaluated nodes gathered by breadth-first traversal from the parent, each shown with the validation score it obtained, as many as fit in the context window, with a high reasoning budget. The judge prompt was optimized with MIPROv2 so that it conducts a structured analysis of each solution and stays tolerant of minor, fixable issues. Nothing is executed before the choice, so the selection adds no GPU time beyond the judge's inference.

title: Efficient RLVR Scheduling via Graph-Structured Online Difficulty Estimation
prompt:
I've been ideating on how sensitive our difficulty estimator is to the strength of the Potts graph prior we use over the latent difficulty assignments. As background, the estimator defines a Potts graph prior over the latent assignments to retain the initial clustering structure while encouraging neighboring samples to share the same latent state: p(\mathbf{z}_t \mid W, A) = \frac{1}{Z(W,A)} \left( \prod_{i=1}^{N} A_{i, z_{i,t}} \right) \exp\left[ \frac{\beta}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} W_{ij} \, \mathbb{I}(z_{i,t} = z_{j,t}) \right], where \mathbf{z}_t = (z_{1,t}, \dots, z_{N,t}) denotes the vector of latent-state assignments at step t, with z_{i,t} \in \{1, \dots, K\} indicating the assignment for sample x_i. The hyperparameter \beta controls the strength of graph propagation, and Z(W,A) is the partition function. K is the number of latent states.

My setup is an ablation on the Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B base model, where I vary \beta and K and measure both sample-level MAE and batch-level Pearson correlation r for the difficulty estimator, evaluated at early and full training steps of RLVR training.

My baseline gets, with the default \beta=2 and K=320: at Early Steps, r = 0.482 Pearson correlation and MAE = 0.29 MAE; at Full Steps, r = 0.836 Pearson correlation and MAE = 0.183 MAE.

title: Efficient RLVR Scheduling via Graph-Structured Online Difficulty Estimation
prompt:
I've been sketching out how much the choice of embedding model matters for the difficulty estimator I'm using in GRPO RL training. The overall setup constructs a sparse similarity graph over the training dataset based on semantic and difficulty features, so that samples with few or no prior rollouts can estimate their current expected difficulty by leveraging historical feedback from semantically and difficulty-wise similar neighbors. To encourage the encoder to capture semantic content, reasoning structure, and difficulty-related characteristics of each sample, I use a difficulty-aware instruction I_\pi: "Instruction: Given a prompt, encode it into a dense vector that captures both its semantic content and difficulty level, for the purpose of similarity comparison. Prompt: [SAMPLE]". Letting f_{\mathrm{emb}} denote a pretrained embedding model, the representation of sample x_i is computed as \widetilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_i = f_{\mathrm{emb}}(I_{\pi}, x_i) and normalized to \boldsymbol{\phi}_i = \widetilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_i / \|\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\phi}}_i\|_2. For each pair of samples, similarity is measured via cosine similarity: c_{ij} = \boldsymbol{\phi}_i^\top \boldsymbol{\phi}_j. To capture the underlying manifold structure of high-dimensional sample embeddings while reducing computational cost, I construct a k-nearest-neighbor graph by retaining the k_{\mathrm{nn}} nearest neighbors of each node, then retain only edges where the two nodes are mutual k-nearest neighbors and remove those with negative similarities, yielding a sparse undirected sample graph. My setup uses Qwen3-0.6B as the sentence embedding model, with K=320, k_{\mathrm{nn}}=80, \gamma=0.5, and \beta=2, applied on top of GRPO RL training with the graph-structured difficulty estimator on Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct base models, where the embeddings are used to build the KNN sample graph. My baseline gets, on MATH with Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B, MAE = 0.183 and r = 0.836 using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B; and on MATH with Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, MAE = 0.131 and r = 0.776 using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B.

title: Efficient RLVR Scheduling via Graph-Structured Online Difficulty Estimation
prompt:
I've been ideating on a windowed forgetting mechanism for the state-level rollout statistics in the graph-structured difficulty estimator. Right now, the online inference procedure accumulates rollout feedback across training steps by inheriting the state-level Beta posterior, i.e. \(a_{k,t}^{\mathrm{hist}}=a_{k,t-1}\) and \(b_{k,t}^{\mathrm{hist}}=b_{k,t-1}\). The concern motivating this is that the rollout distribution is non-stationary since the policy parameters keep changing during RL optimization, so rollout observations collected many training steps earlier may no longer accurately characterize the success probability of the current policy. The windowed mechanism I'm considering keeps the difficulty-aware sample graph \(W\), the smoothed assignment prior \(A\), the Potts graph prior, and the mean-field variational family from the main method unchanged, and only changes how historical rollout evidence is organized: state-level success probabilities would be estimated from a recent sliding window, while the complete rollout history of each previously observed sample is still retained for sample-level prediction. Concretely, instead of directly inheriting the complete Beta posterior from the previous step, the windowed variant reconstructs the state-level Beta parameters from a fixed prior and the rollout evidence within the current window: \begin{align} a_{k,t}^{(L)}=a_0+S_{k,t}^{(L)},\qquad b_{k,t}^{(L)}=b_0+F_{k,t}^{(L)}. \end{align} In my implementation, I set \(a_0=b_0=1\), corresponding to the uniform prior \(\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)\), which is a standard weak prior for a Bernoulli success probability that doesn't favor any particular success rate before rollout evidence is observed, and it guarantees the Beta parameters stay strictly positive -- important since under a finite window some latent states may get no rollout observations in the current window. When \(S_{k,t}^{(L)}=F_{k,t}^{(L)}=0\), the \(\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)\) prior still yields a valid posterior and keeps the posterior mean and the digamma terms used in the variational updates well-defined and numerically stable. Ideally the prior mean \begin{align} \mathbb{E}[\theta_{k,t}]=\frac{a_0}{a_0+b_0} \end{align} should be close to the average success probability of the current policy, which would give a more informative default for latent states with few or no recent observations, but getting a reliable estimate of that would require evaluating a sufficiently large and representative subset of the training set at each stage, adding substantial rollout cost, and estimating it only from scheduler-selected samples would be potentially biased since those samples aren't representative of the full training distribution -- so I adopted \(\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)\) as a practical trade-off among prior neutrality, numerical stability, and computational efficiency. The posterior mean success probability of latent state \(k\) is then \begin{align} \mu_{k,t}^{(L)}=\frac{a_{k,t}^{(L)}}{a_{k,t}^{(L)}+b_{k,t}^{(L)}}. \end{align} The model-based prediction for sample \(x_i\) retains the same mixture form as in the main method: \begin{align} \widehat{p}_{i,t}^{\mathrm{model}}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}q_{ik,t}\mu_{k,t}^{(L)}. \end{align} When the window covers all preceding training steps, this windowed formulation reduces to the cumulative-history variant; with a finite \(L\), rollout observations older than \(L\) training steps no longer directly contribute to the current state-level success probabilities. My setup is to evaluate this windowed variant by replaying the full training logs of Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on the GRPO training runs for the graph-structured difficulty estimator, and compare against the cumulative estimator used in the main experiments, looking at sample-level MAE and the correlation metric \(r\) on the MATH training split for both models. My baseline gets: on the MATH training split with Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B, the cumulative estimator (Ours) has MAE = 0.183 and r = 0.836; on the MATH training split with Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, the cumulative estimator (Ours) has MAE = 0.131 and r = 0.776.

My question about this setup: after switching from Ours (cumulative estimator) (my baseline above) to Windows (windowed variant), predict the resulting value for each: MATH training split (Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B) MAE; MATH training split (Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B) r; MATH training split (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct) MAE; MATH training split (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct) r.
