title: Efficient RLVR Scheduling via Graph-Structured Online Difficulty Estimation
prompt:
I've been sketching out a way to bring a graph-based difficulty estimator into curriculum-selection schedulers for RLVR training, specifically targeting PCL, which is a curriculum-learning method that trains a dedicated difficulty predictor. The idea is to aggregate the state-level posterior from the previous training step into sample-level estimates of success probability (difficulty), which then guide adaptive sample selection. At the beginning of RL training step t, the estimator loads the state $\mathcal{S}_{t-1} = \{q_{t-1}, a_{t-1}, b_{t-1}\}$ from the previous step. For each latent state k, I compute the posterior mean of its success probability as $\mu_{k,t-1} = \frac{a_{k,t-1}}{a_{k,t-1}+b_{k,t-1}}$. I first form a model-based prediction for sample $x_i$: $\widehat{p}_{i,t}^{\text{model}} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} q_{ik,t-1} \mu_{k,t-1}$. Then I adjust the prediction based on whether the sample has been rolled out before: if $x_i$ has no prior rollouts, I directly use the model prediction, $\widehat{p}_{i,t} = \widehat{p}_{i,t}^{\text{model}}$; if it has been sampled in earlier steps, I average the model prediction with its historical success rate $\bar r_{i,<t}$, $\widehat{p}_{i,t} = \gamma \widehat{p}_{i,t}^{\text{model}} + (1-\gamma)\bar r_{i,<t}$, with $\gamma =0.5$. The estimated difficulty is then $\widehat{d}_{i,t} = 1 - \widehat{p}_{i,t}$. Before each training step t, the estimator predicts the difficulty of every sample, and this is meant to serve as a plug-and-play component for sample-level scheduling frameworks like PCL, replacing only the original difficulty estimator while retaining the underlying scheduling strategy. My setup integrates this into PCL's GRPO-style curriculum selection, and I compare against the original PCL under the same total generation budget, using rule-based matching to judge whether a result matches the ground truth. Because a single evaluation on small and challenging datasets such as AIME can be sensitive to sampling randomness, I sample eight independent rollouts per prompt and report Average@8 accuracy. I conduct all training and inference on 4xA100 80G GPUs, using Qwen 2.5 1.5B Math and Llama 3 1B-Instruct as base models, keeping the environment strictly consistent with the original baselines and using the same computational budget across experiments, equivalent to one round of the standard GVM algorithm. My baseline (PCL) currently gets: on Qwen 2.5 1.5B Math, MATH500 Average@8 = 59.7%, AIME24 Average@8 = 7.92%, AIME25 Average@8 = 4.58%, OlympiadBench Average@8 = 26.1%; on Llama 3 1B-Instruct, MATH500 Average@8 = 26.7%, AIME24 Average@8 = 0.42%, AIME25 Average@8 = 0.0%, OlympiadBench Average@8 = 5.04%.

My question about this setup: after switching from PCL (my baseline above) to PCL+Ours, predict the resulting value for each: MATH500 (Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B) Average@8 accuracy (in %); AIME24 (Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B) Average@8 accuracy (in %); AIME25 (Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B) Average@8 accuracy (in %); OlympiadBench (Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B) Average@8 accuracy (in %); MATH500 (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct) Average@8 accuracy (in %); AIME24 (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct) Average@8 accuracy (in %); AIME25 (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct) Average@8 accuracy (in %); OlympiadBench (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct) Average@8 accuracy (in %).

title: Efficient RLVR Scheduling via Graph-Structured Online Difficulty Estimation
prompt:
I've been iterating on a comparison between a historical-feedback statistical estimator (VIP) and an online graph-based estimator for tracking sample difficulty as it evolves during GRPO training. The idea behind the graph-based formulation is to transfer feedback across related samples in order to address observation sparsity in the early stage of training, whereas VIP relies purely on accumulated historical feedback per sample without that structural sharing. My setup follows the same evaluation protocol across both methods: at each evaluation point in a GRPO training trajectory (batch size 256), I use the empirical success rate from 8 independent rollouts generated by the current policy as the reference empirical success probability. I train on Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, and I track difficulty estimation quality at Early, Middle, Last, and Full training steps. I report sample-level MAE for calibration and batch-level Pearson correlation r (batch size 256) for ranking consistency, since sample-level empirical rates are discrete and sparse — lower MAE and higher r indicate better estimation. The RL training data comes from NuminaMath, a large-scale mathematical reasoning dataset of approximately 860K problem-solution pairs covering problems from Chinese high-school mathematics to US and international olympiad competitions, with chain-of-thought solutions and verifiable final answers; following the data-processing protocols of GVM and CurES, I extract approximately 150K problems from this corpus for RL training. My baseline for VIP currently gets, on Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B: Early Steps MAE = 0.373; Middle Steps MAE = 0.094, r = 0.794; Last Steps MAE = 0.084, r = 0.885; Full Steps MAE = 0.184, r = 0.423; with an estimation time cost of 0.05 A100*h. On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, VIP gets: Early Steps MAE = 0.413; Middle Steps MAE = 0.107, r = 0.895; Last Steps MAE = 0.084, r = 0.88; Full Steps MAE = 0.201, r = 0.717; with time cost of 0.05 A100*h.

title: Efficient RLVR Scheduling via Graph-Structured Online Difficulty Estimation
prompt:
I've been sketching out a way to initialize the latent-state assignments in a graph-structured online difficulty estimator using spectral clustering rather than random initialization. The idea is that we apply spectral clustering to the sparse undirected sample graph $W \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}$ to get an initial set of static cluster labels $c_i \in \{1,\ldots,K\}$. Since spectral clustering relies solely on static sample representations, and its assignments can be affected by representation and clustering errors, and since the difficulty of the same sample under the current policy may change as we continuously update the policy during RL training, I convert each static cluster label into a smoothed prior distribution over latent states, defined as $\displaystyle A_{ik}=\begin{cases}1-\epsilon, & k=c_i,\\\frac{\epsilon}{K-1}, & k\neq c_i,\end{cases}$. This is meant to retain the structure from spectral clustering while still allowing subsequent rollout outcomes to refine each sample's latent assignment.　My setup evaluates this over the full GRPO training trajectory on two models, Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, trained on NuminaMath. I report sample-level MAE for calibration and batch-level Pearson correlation $r$ (batch size 256) for ranking consistency, since sample-level empirical rates are discrete and sparse; lower MAE and higher $r$ indicate better estimation. My baseline, without spectral initialization, gets: for Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B, sample-level MAE (↓) = 0.218 and Pearson correlation r (↑) = 0.71; for Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, sample-level MAE (↓) = 0.197 and Pearson correlation r (↑) = 0.686.

title: Efficient RLVR Scheduling via Graph-Structured Online Difficulty Estimation
prompt:
I've been working on a graph-structured online difficulty estimator that tracks latent-state assignments for samples across the full GRPO training trajectory, and one piece I'm exploring is a Potts-prior smoothing mechanism over those latent assignments. The idea is to introduce a Potts graph prior over the latent-state assignments that retains the initial clustering structure while encouraging neighboring samples to share the same latent state. Specifically, the prior is defined as p(\mathbf{z}_t \mid W, A) = \frac{1}{Z(W,A)} \left( \prod_{i=1}^{N} A_{i, z_{i,t}} \right) \exp\left[ \frac{\beta}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} W_{ij} \, \mathbb{I}(z_{i,t} = z_{j,t}) \right], where \mathbf{z}_t = (z_{1,t}, \dots, z_{N,t}) denotes the vector of latent-state assignments at step t, with z_{i,t} \in \{1, \dots, K\} indicating the assignment for sample x_i. The hyperparameter \beta controls the strength of graph propagation. My motivation for this design is that as the policy evolves, sample difficulty and its latent-state assignment should evolve accordingly, and a smoothed prior on A_{ik} is meant to preserve the initial clustering structure while still allowing rollout feedback to revise the assignments over time, as opposed to using hard assignments which would prevent that kind of adaptation.

My setup uses Qwen 2.5 1.5B Math and Llama 3 1B-Instruct as base models. I keep the environment strictly consistent with the original baselines, integrating this as a plug-and-play component into the original code, and I use the same computational budget across all experiments, equivalent to one round of the standard GVM algorithm (~1.5M rollouts, including pre-sampling). I use Qwen3-0.6B as the sentence embedding model, with K=320, k_{\mathrm{nn}}=80, \gamma=0.5, and \beta=2. Since all the baselines I'm integrating with are based on mathematical problems, I conduct reinforcement learning on NuminaMath, following prior experimental settings.

My baseline currently gets, for Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B on the NuminaMath full trajectory without prior smoothing: sample-level MAE of 0.197 and a Pearson correlation r of 0.783. For Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on the NuminaMath full trajectory without prior smoothing: sample-level MAE of 0.144 and a Pearson correlation r of 0.736.

title: Efficient RLVR Scheduling via Graph-Structured Online Difficulty Estimation
prompt:
I've been iterating on the graph construction side of my online difficulty estimator, specifically looking at graph sparsification of the sample similarity graph. The idea is to build a k-nearest-neighbor graph by retaining the k_{\mathrm{nn}} nearest neighbors of each node, then keep only edges where the two nodes are mutual k-nearest neighbors and remove those with negative similarities, which yields a sparse undirected sample graph. The motivation is that a dense graph can introduce weakly related edges that add noise into feedback propagation, whereas sparsification should retain more reliable relationships between samples for propagating rollout feedback. My setup is a graph-structured online difficulty estimator evaluated over the full GRPO training trajectory, tested on both Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on the NuminaMath dataset, with sample-level MAE and Pearson correlation r as the metrics. I'm running this as part of a broader ablation that also covers spectral initialization and prior smoothing, but here I'm focused on the sparsification component. My baseline without graph sparsification gets: for Qwen-2.5-Math-1.5B on NuminaMath full trajectory, MAE = 0.187 sample-level MAE and r = 0.835 Pearson correlation; for Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on NuminaMath full trajectory, MAE = 0.134 sample-level MAE and r = 0.742 Pearson correlation.

title: StagedWorkspace: A Versioned Workspace for Knowledge-Work Agents
prompt:
I've been iterating on the read-axis design of StagedWorkspace, specifically around how the agent accesses evidence during multi-step office document tasks. The core idea is dual artifact access: exposing two synchronized read paths over the same workspace state $W_t$, where parsed views support evidence localization (parsed search and parsed reads across large document collections) and native artifacts support faithful inspection, execution, and editing (preserving layout, formulas, and executable office files). Because both paths derive from the same workspace state, the agent should be able to search a parsed cache and then open or execute the corresponding native file without crossing artifact versions.

My setup is a read-axis ablation comparing three access arms: dual, which exposes both the native working tree $W_t$ and the hash-keyed parsed cache $C_t$; artifact-only, which exposes only $W_t$; and parsed-only, which exposes only $C_t$. Records in $C_t$ are keyed to their source paths and content hashes, and a record whose source hash no longer matches the corresponding file in $W_t$ is marked stale until refreshed. Dual and parsed-only share the same parsed index, while artifact-only disables access to the parsed index. I hold file tracking, prompts, parser, retriever, grader, and tool budget fixed across all arms, and I run this fixed-harness ablation on OfficeQA Pro across three LLM backends: GPT-5.4, Gemini 3 Flash, and Gemini 3.1 Pro, all under a common agent harness.

For the artifact-only arm, which is my current baseline for this ablation, on OfficeQA Pro with GPT-5.4 I get Accuracy (Pass@1) of 52.6%, Latency of 8.1min, Cost of 0.85$, and Tools count of 34.7. With Gemini 3 Flash, artifact-only gets Accuracy (Pass@1) of 47.7%, Latency of 16.9min, Cost of 0.53$, and Tools count of 41.7. With Gemini 3.1 Pro, artifact-only gets Accuracy (Pass@1) of 55.6%, Latency of 8.6min, Cost of 0.71$, and Tools count of 33.6.

My question about this setup: after switching from Artifact-only (my baseline above) to Dual, predict the resulting value for each: OfficeQA Pro (GPT-5.4) Accuracy (Pass@1) (in %); OfficeQA Pro (GPT-5.4) Latency (min) (in min); OfficeQA Pro (GPT-5.4) Cost ($) (in $); OfficeQA Pro (GPT-5.4) Tools (in count); OfficeQA Pro (Gemini 3 Flash) Accuracy (Pass@1) (in %); OfficeQA Pro (Gemini 3 Flash) Latency (min) (in min); OfficeQA Pro (Gemini 3 Flash) Cost ($) (in $); OfficeQA Pro (Gemini 3 Flash) Tools (in count); OfficeQA Pro (Gemini 3.1 Pro) Accuracy (Pass@1) (in %); OfficeQA Pro (Gemini 3.1 Pro) Latency (min) (in min); OfficeQA Pro (Gemini 3.1 Pro) Cost ($) (in $); OfficeQA Pro (Gemini 3.1 Pro) Tools (in count).

title: StagedWorkspace: A Versioned Workspace for Knowledge-Work Agents
prompt:
I've been developing a workspace mechanism I'm calling visible workspace review diffs, aimed at giving an agent a compact chance to compare its intended edits against actual file changes before it submits its work. The idea is that even though a diff doesn't prove semantic correctness, exposing it could let the model catch discrepancies between what it meant to do and what actually happened on disk.

To test this, I set up a paired review-axis ablation on a 57-task file-editing subset of APEX-Agents (roughly 12% of the full benchmark). Both conditions in this ablation hold the dual-view workspace configuration fixed and use identical file tracking, recording the same underlying file changes in both arms. The only difference is whether the agent can inspect those tracked changes before submission: in the diff-visible arm, the agent is exposed to workspace_diff and workspace_file_diff before submitting, while in the diff-hidden arm it is not. I excluded OfficeQA from this ablation since it scores final text answers rather than edited files, so only the file-editing tasks in APEX are used. I ran this across three agent models: Gemini 3 Flash High, GPT-5.4 Mini xHigh, and GPT-5.4 Nano xHigh, all under the same dual-view workspace setup.

My baseline (diffs hidden) results on the 57 file-editing tasks are: Gemini 3 Flash High gets a mean rubric score of 47.6 points, GPT-5.4 Mini xHigh gets a mean rubric score of 40.9 points, and GPT-5.4 Nano xHigh gets a mean rubric score of 48.1 points.

title: StagedWorkspace: A Versioned Workspace for Knowledge-Work Agents
prompt:
I've been iterating on how the parsed-document cache is kept in sync with the underlying files in StagedWorkspace, since the OfficeQA agents rely on dual artifact views: a parsed read path for evidence localization across large document collections, and a native read path for faithful inspection, execution, and editing. The idea I'm working through is keeping the parsed cache as derived state rather than a static export. Each parsed record is keyed to the source path and a content hash, so when sandbox synchronization observes a changed hash, only the affected parsed records get marked stale and queued for refresh, while unchanged files reuse their prior parsed records. The motivation is to stop vector search, grep, and parsed reads from surfacing evidence off an earlier file version as if it were current, which is exactly the failure mode of a static, non-hash-synced parse. My setup contrasts this live hash-keyed parsed cache with hydrated PDFs against the static release parse without hash sync: the latter is OfficeQA's published Databricks .txt export, built from parsed elements from Databricks ai_parse_document concatenated in reading order with figures omitted, which ships no live PDFs, no post-edit re-index, and no native execution on the eval workspace. My primary parsed-only and dual arms instead use live Reducto parsing over hydrated PDFs with hash-keyed re-indexing and the defined tool routes, while the Databricks .txt baseline is retained only as a leaderboard-aligned efficiency comparison under the StagedWorkspace harness on OfficeQA Pro. My baseline (Parsed-only, Databricks) currently gets, for GPT-5.4: Accuracy 60.2%, Latency 7.9min, Cost $0.94, Tools 30.6 tool calls; for Gemini 3 Flash: Accuracy 52.6%, Latency 11.6min, Cost $0.71, Tools 54.5 tool calls; and for Gemini 3.1 Pro: Accuracy 52.6%, Latency 7.3min, Cost $0.78, Tools 26.7 tool calls.

title: Adaptive Multi-Agent Feature Selection for Personalized Fall Risk Prevention
prompt:
I've been ideating on how to encode multi-level structural dependencies among features within the PAFIR framework, building on the hierarchical distance structure encoding (HDSE) idea. The core mechanism: structurally informed features are derived by applying hierarchical structure encoding, which reveals and encodes latent multi-level feature relationships among features and their association with the primary outcome. At each visit, each node represents a feature (e.g., BMI, weight, height), and each feature group (e.g., body composition) forms a fully connected graph $\mathcal{G}_m = (\mathcal{V}_m, \mathcal{E}_m)$, where $\mathcal{V}_m$ is the set of features belonging to group $m$. I construct a multi-level hierarchy for each feature group by iteratively coarsening the graph to generate $K+1$ levels. At each level $k$, I compute the graph hierarchy distance (GHD) between nodes $v \in \mathcal{V}_m$ and $u \in \mathcal{V}_m$, denoted as,
\begin{align*}
    \text{GHD}^{k}(v,u)
    =
    \text{SPD}\!\left(
    \psi_{k-1} \circ \cdots \circ \psi_0(v),
    \psi_{k-1} \circ \cdots \circ \psi_0(u)
    \right),
\end{align*}
where $\psi_{k-1} \circ \cdots \circ \psi_0(v)$ is the mapping of node $v$ from level $0$ to level $k$ in the graph hierarchy, and $\text{SPD}(\cdot, \cdot)$ denotes shortest path distance.

For each feature node $v$, I construct a structural distance tensor $\mathbf{D}_v \in \mathbb{R}^{(K+1) \times |\mathcal{V}_m|}$ by stacking its pairwise distances to all other nodes $u \in \mathcal{V}_m$ across all hierarchy levels. Each entry $\mathbf{D}_{v,u}$ captures the multi-level distances from node $v$ to node $u$,
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{D}_{v,u}
=
\left[
\text{GHD}^{0}(v,u),
\text{GHD}^{1}(v,u),
\cdots,
\text{GHD}^{K}(v,u)
\right].
\end{equation}
This tensor captures the multi-level structural relationships of node $v$ within group $m$. To obtain a compact representation, I apply positional encoding to $\mathbf{D}_v$, yielding a dense embedding that encodes the hierarchical position of the feature.

My setup is to evaluate the effectiveness of this hierarchical graph encoder in capturing structural dependencies by performing an ablation that removes this component from the PAFIR architecture, evaluated on graph benchmark datasets for both node and graph classification tasks. For graph benchmarks, I follow the data-processing and split protocol of TAR. Each experiment is repeated 10 times with different random seeds, and the mean performance is reported. For graph-based tasks, I evaluate the quality of the transformed feature space using Precision, Recall, and F1 score, where higher values indicate better performance.

My baseline, without hierarchical graph encoding, gets: on PROTEINS, Node Classification Precision = 0.678, Recall = 0.673, F1 Score = 0.675; Graph Classification Precision = 0.765, Recall = 0.757, F1 Score = 0.766. On ENZYMES, Node Classification Precision = 0.926, Recall = 0.923, F1 Score = 0.927; Graph Classification Precision = 0.34, Recall = 0.344, F1 Score = 0.348. On AIDS, Node Classification Precision = 0.896, Recall = 0.863, F1 Score = 0.884; Graph Classification Precision = 0.808, Recall = 0.82, F1 Score = 0.814.

My question about this setup: after switching from w/o Hierarchical Graph Encoding (my baseline above) to PAFIR (Full), predict the resulting value for each: PROTEINS - Node Classification Precision (in score); PROTEINS - Node Classification Recall (in score); PROTEINS - Node Classification F1 Score (in score); PROTEINS - Graph Classification Precision (in score); PROTEINS - Graph Classification Recall (in score); PROTEINS - Graph Classification F1 Score (in score); ENZYMES - Node Classification Precision (in score); ENZYMES - Node Classification Recall (in score); ENZYMES - Node Classification F1 Score (in score); ENZYMES - Graph Classification Precision (in score); ENZYMES - Graph Classification Recall (in score); ENZYMES - Graph Classification F1 Score (in score); AIDS - Node Classification Precision (in score); AIDS - Node Classification Recall (in score); AIDS - Node Classification F1 Score (in score); AIDS - Graph Classification Precision (in score); AIDS - Graph Classification Recall (in score); AIDS - Graph Classification F1 Score (in score).

title: Adaptive Multi-Agent Feature Selection for Personalized Fall Risk Prevention
prompt:
I've been brainstorming about how to do adaptive feature selection over hierarchical, multimodal longitudinal data using a multi-agent RL approach, which is the core idea behind what I'm calling PAFIR. The motivation is to dynamically identify fall risk factors across repeated clinical visits by combining structured clinical assessments with continuous wearable sensor streams, using sparse and delayed fall incidence signals plus proxy outcomes to guide learning.

My setup uses longitudinal, multimodal data from the PEER study, with 341 community-dwelling participants assessed at four time points (1,364 participant-visit observations). After each scheduled visit, participants wore sensors for seven consecutive days, generating minute-level wearable data totaling over 2.5 million time-stamped observations across all participants and visits. At each visit, participants also contribute high-dimensional structured clinical assessments spanning physical, cognitive, psychological, and functional domains; after preprocessing this structured modality comprises 587 fall-related features organized into 35 clinically meaningful feature groups (e.g., body composition, physical activity, cognitive function, balance confidence, psychological status). Each participant-visit instance is modeled as a graph-structured input.

The structured feature space is encoded using a six-layer graph encoder with hidden dimension 128, residual connections, and dropout rate 0.5, with mean pooling and Laplacian positional encoding (up to ten eigenvectors) applied to aggregate node-level representations. In parallel, minute-level wearable sensor data (step counts, vector magnitude (VM), and posture states: sitting, standing, lying) are processed by a temporal encoder using four stacked Transformer encoder blocks, each with four attention heads and a feed-forward dimension of 256, with wearable inputs projected through a shared linear embedding layer. The resulting temporal representations are aligned with visit-level structured embeddings and fused via a cross-attention Transformer module, producing a hierarchical latent state that feeds the reinforcement learning component. RL-based feature selection operates at the visit level or when a fall incidence occurs, letting the model update feature importance dynamically as new temporal and structural information becomes available. Fall incidence events are recorded as self-reported, time-stamped outcomes providing sparse, delayed supervision, alongside FES-I and BBS proxy outcomes used in reward calculation.

The model is trained for 100 epochs using the Adam optimizer with learning rate 0.001. The Q-network of each agent is optimized using a temporal-difference loss, and binary cross-entropy loss is used for the fall-outcome classification model employed in the fall-based reward calculation. Experiments run on NVIDIA Quadro RTX 6000 GPUs using CUDA 13.0, with each random-seed run taking approximately 101 seconds and the complete 20-seed longitudinal stability analysis taking approximately 34 minutes; peak allocated GPU memory is approximately 240 MB.

I'm comparing PAFIR against several prior feature selection baselines: TAR, SAT, TTG, PCA, Group LASSO, and LASSO. Participants are randomly divided into 80% training and 20% testing sets, with all longitudinal observations from the same participant kept in the same partition, and all data-dependent quantities (feature-importance scores, inter-group correlations) estimated using only the training partition. All experiments are repeated 20 times with different random seeds, with results reported as mean ± standard deviation. I'm assessing feature selection quality using four metrics: Feature Recovery Rate (FRR), False Discovery Rate (FDR), Selection Stability, and Correlation Recovery.

My baseline, TAR, on the PEER study for fall risk factor selection gets FRR = 0.795, FDR = 0.209, Selection Stability = 0.989, and Correlation Recovery = 0.973 (means over 20 seeds).

title: Adaptive Multi-Agent Feature Selection for Personalized Fall Risk Prevention
prompt:
I've been developing a hierarchical multimodal structure encoding component within the PAFIR framework, aimed at capturing both within-domain and cross-domain relationships in longitudinal clinical and physical activity data. The idea is to partition the feature space $\mathcal{X}$ into $M$ clinically meaningful feature sets $\{\mathcal{V}_1,\mathcal{V}_2,\dots,\mathcal{V}_M\}$, where each $\mathcal{V}_m\subseteq\mathcal{X}$ groups related features (e.g., body composition variables like BMI and weight, physical functional measures like grip strength, or psychological assessments like FES for fear of falling), with $\bigcup_{m=1}^{M}\mathcal{V}_m=\mathcal{X}$. Within each group, I represent features as nodes in an intra-group graph $\mathcal{G}_m=(\mathcal{V}_m,\mathcal{E}_m)$, where the groups follow the predefined PEER assessment domains and every pair of features within the same domain is fully connected, encoding shared clinical-domain membership. Across groups, I define an inter-group topology $\mathcal{T} = (\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{W})$, where each node $u_m \in \mathcal{U}$ represents a feature group $\mathcal{V}_m$. For participant $i$ at update $t$, I compute $\Phi_{i,t}^{(m)} = \sum_{v\in \mathcal{V}_m}\phi_{i,t,v}$ as the initial importance score of group $m$, where $\phi_{i,t,v}$ is the importance of feature $v$; these scores initialize the structural representation, the reward reference, and the feature-selection process. Each weighted edge $w_{mn} \in \mathcal{W}$ captures co-variation in initial importance between groups $m$ and $n$, computed as $w_{mn} = \operatorname{Corr}_{(i,t)\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}}\!\left(\Phi_{i,t}^{(m)}, \Phi_{i,t}^{(n)}\right)$ over available participant-update observations in the training data. For each feature $v \in \mathcal{V}_m$, I construct a structural representation $\mathbf{h}_{i,t,v}$ capturing its relationships with other features in the same clinical domain for participant $i$ at update $t$, and I collect these into $\mathbf{H}_{i,t} = \left\{\mathbf{h}_{i,t,v}: v\in\mathcal{V}_m,\; m=1,\ldots,M \right\}$ at each update. My setup applies this within the PAFIR framework to longitudinal multimodal PEER trial data for fall risk feature selection. Participants are randomly divided into 80% training and 20% testing sets, with all longitudinal observations from the same participant kept within the same partition, and all data-dependent quantities (feature-importance scores and inter-group correlations) estimated using only the training partition. title: Adaptive Multi-Agent Feature Selection for Personalized Fall Risk Prevention
prompt:
I've been iterating on the reward formulation inside PAFIR, specifically the sparse-aware reward component that's supposed to handle the fact that fall incidence is such a sparse and temporally irregular signal in the PEER data. The idea is that many participants never fall across their visits, so if the reward only depended on fall occurrence, feedback would be extremely limited and delayed. My design instead builds a dynamic reward: baseline feature-importance scores initialize the reward reference and selection prior, and during training the reward is computed from whatever outcome information is available at each update. When a fall occurs between visits, the reward is adjusted immediately based on how much the selected features contributed, with feature groups more strongly associated with fall risk getting higher rewards and non-contributing ones penalized. At scheduled assessment updates where no fall feedback exists, the reward instead uses a clinical proxy like FES-I or BBS, which are collected at every visit. The reward function is r_{i,t} = \operatorname{Perf}\left(F_{i,t},y_{i,t}\right) - p_{i,t-1}, where \operatorname{Perf}(F_{i,t},y_{i,t}) is the evaluation measure for the fall outcome when fall feedback is available and for the proxy outcome otherwise, and p_{i,t-1} is the best previously observed performance for that type of feedback. Each agent (cand, ref, op) is trained with its own deep Q-network, with temporal-difference loss \mathcal{L}_{i,t}^{(j)} = \Bigg( Q_j\left(\mathbf{s}_{i,t},a_{i,t}^{(j)}\right) - \bigg[ r_{i,t} + \gamma \max_{a'} Q_j\left(\mathbf{s}_{i,t+1},a'\right) \bigg] \Bigg)^2, where Q_j is agent j's action-value function, a_{i,t}^{(j)} its action, r_{i,t} the shared reward, and \gamma the discount factor. All Q-networks are randomly initialized and trained with this loss, and the baseline feature-importance scores initialize both the reward and the initial feature selection. My setup uses the PEER study's longitudinal, multimodal fall prevention data: 341 community-dwelling participants assessed at four time points, giving 1,364 participant-visit observations. At each visit participants wore sensors for seven consecutive days, producing minute-level wearable data totaling over 2.5 million time-stamped observations. Structured clinical assessments after preprocessing yield 587 fall-related features organized into 35 clinically meaningful feature groups spanning body composition, physical activity, cognitive function, balance confidence, and psychological status. Each participant-visit is modeled as a graph-structured input encoded by a graph encoder, while minute-level wearable data (step counts, vector magnitude, and posture states like sitting, standing, lying) is processed by a time-series encoder; the two are fused via a cross-attention Transformer module into a hierarchical latent state feeding the reinforcement learning component. Fall incidence is self-reported and time-stamped, giving sparse, delayed supervision, while FES-I and BBS proxy scores are assessed at every visit. I evaluate with participants randomly split 80% train / 20% test, keeping all longitudinal observations from the same participant in one partition, with all data-dependent quantities (feature-importance scores, inter-group correlations) estimated only from the training partition. I repeat this 20 times with different random seeds and report mean results across four metrics: Feature Recovery Rate (FRR), False Discovery Rate (FDR), Selection Stability, and Correlation Recovery. My baseline, without the sparse-aware reward component, currently gets FRR = 0.655 fraction, FDR = 0.325 fraction, Selection Stability = 0.665 fraction, and Correlation Recovery = 0.701 fraction on the PEER study data.

My question about this setup: after switching from w/o Sparse-Aware Rewards (my baseline above) to PAFIR (Full), predict the resulting value for each: PEER study FRR (in fraction); PEER study FDR (in fraction); PEER study Selection Stability (in fraction); PEER study Correlation Recovery (in fraction).

title: The Role of Grid Cells in Reducing Spatial Aliasing in Hippocampal Place Representations
prompt:
I've been working on integrating grid cells into a place cell representation to see how they interact with boundary vector cell (BVC) inputs when disambiguating spatially similar locations. The core idea is that place cells integrate two input streams: BVCs provide geometric constraints from environmental boundaries, while grid cells (GCs) contribute metric phase information that can disambiguate perceptually similar locations. The relative contribution of these two streams is controlled by a weighting parameter η ∈ [0,1], where BVC inputs are weighted by (1-η) and GC inputs by η.

My setup uses an analytical grid cell and BVC-driven place cell model with 8 head-direction cells, 400 BVCs, grid cells divided into 8 modules of 50 cells each (400 grid cells total, spatial scale λ=5.5, giving an activation diameter of roughly 2.7m), and 1000 place cells, trained via competitive Oja-rule learning while the agent explores. The agent is a Roomba-like bot in Webots with a compass for head-direction updates and a rangefinder with 720 beams covering 360 degrees (max range 25m) feeding into the BVC layer, and all environments used are 20m x 20m in size. For the open environment, 5 trials were run for each configuration (with and without grid cells), with training continuing until 95 percent coverage was reached (0.5m bin size) and evaluation continuing until 99 percent coverage was reached (0.2m bin size, matching the bin size used for the Mean Spatial Aliasing Index, MSAI, metric). In the no grid cell condition, η is set to 0 so that BVC inputs alone drive the place cell layer.

My baseline in the open environment with no GC (η=0, BVC-only) gets an MSAI of 5.7×10⁻⁴.

title: Learned, Then Lost: A Measured Single-Example Counterfactual in Pre-training
prompt:
I've been iterating on how sensitive our interpolation loss barrier metric is to the amount of held-out data we evaluate it on, since that's our primary registered dependent variable and I want to make sure it isn't an artifact of a small evaluation window. As background, my setup trains GPT-2 at 124M parameters from scratch on OpenWebText, using a corpus of 2,499,805,184 training tokens and 10,485,760 held-out tokens, with 9,536 total steps per pre-training run and a 200-step warmup during which learning rate ramps to its 6e-4 peak; injections are placed at peak learning rate (step 200) deliberately. The barrier itself is computed by taking the finished weights of a run and its seed-matched twin, walking the straight line between them at 21 evenly spaced points, evaluating held-out cross-entropy at each point, and taking the maximum departure from the chord connecting the two endpoint losses. title: Learned, Then Lost: A Measured Single-Example Counterfactual in Pre-training
prompt:
I've been working on an idea around attested-subject content injection — basically manipulating truth/attestation status of an injected subject rather than fluency or form, and seeing whether that distinction shows up in downstream training dynamics. The two fluent passages we compare are matched in register and structure, both 194 tokens long, and differ only in whether the subject is corpus-attested (Jimmie Nicol, who appears 4 times in the training corpus) or fabricated (Gizmo Harrington, who appears zero times, counts taken before any run existed). The attested subject is also the one whose passage happens to be true, so anything a contrast between the two picks up can't be pinned on attestation alone, since truth rides along with it. Fluent-attested/fluent-fabricated names how the passages were constructed, and the model-side variable the contrast manipulates is whether the subject is attested in the training corpus.

My setup is 32 GPT-2 (124M parameter) models trained from scratch on OpenWebText, split into 4 conditions x 8 seeds. Each model is trained from an initialization of random weights (dictated by the seed), using a corpus of 2,499,805,184 training tokens and 10,485,760 held-out tokens, both from OpenWebText. There are 9,536 total steps in each pre-training run, with warmup of 200 steps so learning rate first reaches its 6e-4 peak at step 200. I inject at peak learning rate deliberately, defined as the maximum update-step size. The injection replaces one row of a 256-row batch outright at step 200, using a fixed 1024-token context (identical across arms and seeds) carrying the 194-token passage at position 400. Because the injected row replaces a whole row, an arm and its twin differ across the entire row while two arms differ only in the 194-token span — which is why the passage-specific analyses contrast two arms against each other rather than an arm against its twin. The row's slot within the batch is derived from the seed (75, 191, 229, 129, 19, 44, 192, 93), while the row's contents are not, so all across-seed spread comes from the models rather than the stimulus.

We matched full-batch gradient delta (the quantity that actually reaches the optimizer when the row is swapped) as the target across fluent arms: 0.010698 for fluent-fabricated and 0.010683 for fluent-attested, a 0.14\%\ difference. Sequence-level norm (the row's own gradient strength) is reported alongside but wasn't the matching target: 2.1521 vs 2.1496, a 0.11\%\ difference. random-chars sits at 0.011788 with cosine 0.790 relative to the other two arms, marking it as a different kind of perturbation moving in a variant direction. Measured against the seed-matched twin at the injected step, the change in full-batch gradient norm is +0.00049, +0.00063, and +0.00050 for fluent-fabricated, fluent-attested, and random-chars respectively, against a twin norm of 0.518 — about 0.1\%\ for all three arms, much smaller than the 2.2\%\ figure from the matching table, since that table reports the norm of the gradient difference, which is largely orthogonal to the batch gradient.

My primary registered variable is interpolation loss barrier: I take the finished weights of a run and its seed-matched twin, walk the straight line between them at 21 evenly spaced points, evaluate held-out cross-entropy at each, and calculate the barrier as the maximum departure from the chord between the two endpoint losses. The held-out section is text carved out before training that no model ever saw, and neither subject appears in it, so the measurement is blind to the manipulation. I use 512 held-out windows, each a 1024-token strip taken as the contiguous non-overlapping prefix of the held-out split. My registered secondary variable is held-out cross-entropy itself. Each condition's displacement is measured from its seed-matched twin on both variables at the final checkpoints; the two fluent conditions are each differenced from their own twin first, then those differences are differenced against each other within seed. One confirmatory comparison was registered (fluent-fabricated minus fluent-attested on interpolation loss barrier), so no multiple-comparison correction applies.

My baseline currently gets, for the fluent-attested (corpus-attested subject) arm measured against its seed-matched twin, an interpolation loss barrier (mean displacement from twin over the 8 seeds) of 0.1462 barrier units.

My question about this setup: after switching from fluent-attested (corpus-attested subject) (my baseline above) to fluent-fabricated (fabricated subject), predict the resulting value for each: Interpolation loss barrier vs seed-matched twin Loss barrier (mean displacement from twin) (in barrier units).

prompt:
I've been iterating on a multi-space coordinated learning framework, UHDformer++, aimed at UHD image deblurring, and comparing it against prior UHD deblurring approaches including UHDformer. The overall architecture operates across 4 coordinated spaces: (a) High-Resolution space (HR), (b) Low-Resolution space (LR), (c) Super-Resolution space (SR), and (d) Low-High Fusion and Reconstruction space (LHFR). HR extracts multi-level high-resolution features and fuses them with low-resolution cues to predict residual images. title: RECOUNT: Reference-guided Counting with Synthetic Visual Exemplars
prompt:
I've been ideating on a way to extend CountGD's zero-shot counting to fine-grained, multi-category settings by adding an image-guided exemplar module (RECOUNT) on top of it, rather than fine-tuning the base counter in-domain. The idea is: at inference time, given a target category and its support set plus a test image, the frozen CountGD counter (pre-trained on FSC-147, prompted with broad category text, using its default preprocessing of shortest side 800, max side 1333) proposes candidate points, one per detected object. My task is to decide which of those belong to the target category. I pool and project each candidate into an embedding P_\theta(f_p), and reduce the support set to a positive gallery \mathcal{G}^+ of target prototypes and a negative gallery \mathcal{G}^- of distractor prototypes (one prototype per exemplar). A candidate is accepted when it more closely resembles the target than any distractor:
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{accept}(p) = \big[\, s^+(p) > s^-(p) \,\big], \qquad
s^+(p) = \max_{g \in \mathcal{G}^+} \langle P_\theta(f_p), P_\theta(g)\rangle, \quad
s^-(p) = \max_{g \in \mathcal{G}^-} \langle P_\theta(f_p), P_\theta(g)\rangle,
\end{equation}
and the predicted count is the number of accepted candidates. This is a nearest-exemplar rule: the single closest prototype across both galleries decides each candidate's label, with no per-category threshold to tune. Specifying a new target just swaps \mathcal{G}^+ and \mathcal{G}^-, leaving the counter, backbone, and P_\theta untouched.

To specify which category to count without annotating the target image, I run the same engine online: from a single reference image per category, I synthesize a support set of synthetic visual exemplars (SVEs), giving a gallery of target SVEs alongside visually similar distractor categories. A support set has two sides: a positive gallery of SVEs depicting the target, and a negative gallery of SVEs for each distractor. Distractors are drawn the same way as during training, as the target's siblings in the taxonomy or as distractors enumerated with the query. I use a gallery rather than a single reference because the SVEs span the target's appearance, poses, lighting, and arrangements, so an object in the scene need only resemble one exemplar to be recognized as the target, whereas a lone reference captures a single view and generalizes poorly. The support set requires no manual annotations on the target image, is built once per category and reused across all of that category's images, and leaves the model itself unchanged.

My setup is: I construct category galleries by synthesizing k=12 SVEs per category using FLUX.2-klein-4B (4 denoising steps at 1024×1024 resolution), conditioned on a single external reference image per category retrieved off-scene from the web (never the query image), prompted using diverse crowd-composition templates completed once per category via an external LLM. Each category is generated from a template "A photograph of {object} {setting}, {arrangement|crowd-composition}. {camera}, {lighting}," appended with a fixed exclusivity clause enforcing a single object type and individually countable instances, with additional scene descriptions drawn from an LLM-generated dictionary of archetypes covering broad categories like birds, produce, office supplies, etc. Negative galleries follow the identical generation pipeline over a curated set of relevant distractors. I adopt the provided positive and negative class lists for each dataset; for LookAlikes, since ground-truth annotations label all instances matching the broad category but group unnamed objects into an "other" bucket, I prompt an LLM to generate a small set of co-occurring distractor categories (e.g., pairing Goldfields as a distractor for California Poppies), and I use this identical set of positive and negative classes across all baselines when benchmarking on LookAlikes.

Each SVE image is processed through CountGD and the frozen vision backbone. Foreground point features are extracted via bilinear interpolation over the patch grid and averaged across detected instances, producing one 768-d prototype per SVE image, so a category gallery consists of the resulting set of 12 prototypes. Query image points are extracted analogously via bilinear sampling at the proposed coordinate. The only trainable component is a lightweight, category-agnostic residual projection head: a 2-layer MLP (768→768) with dropout (0.1), residual skip connections, and \ell_2-normalized outputs, applied identically to query point features and gallery prototypes, functioning as a category-agnostic feature purifier rather than a parameterized classifier.

The projection head is trained using a multi-negative InfoNCE objective (temperature \tau=0.07) on my SynthAlikes dataset. For each query prototype, the positive target is its corresponding gallery, while the denominator comprises all same-group sibling galleries plus n=2 sampled cross-group negatives, regularized by a dispersion loss (weight 0.02). I optimize using AdamW (learning rate 5×10^{-5}, weight decay 10^{-4}, batch size 8) for 1 epoch on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU over the SynthAlikes point annotations. Because the vision backbone and CountGD counter remain frozen throughout, only the ~1.2M parameters of the residual projection head are updated.

I evaluate this in a domain adaptation setting, transferring CountGD from FSC147 to either the LookAlikes or PairTally datasets, treating the approach as an image-guided zero-shot method since category specification at inference requires only a single reference image per category, reusable across any arbitrary query image, and not dependent on human-annotated exemplars on the query image itself. My baseline for CountGD (Text, Zero-Shot) on LookAlikes (A→B) gets an MAE of 30.17 count error and an RMSE of 45.01 count error, and on PairTally (A→C) gets an MAE of 50.32 count error (the table reports no RMSE for this baseline on PairTally).

My question about this setup: after switching from CountGD (Text, Zero-Shot) (my baseline above) to CountGD + RECOUNT (Image, Zero-Shot), predict the resulting value for each: LookAlikes (A→B) MAE (in count error); LookAlikes (A→B) RMSE (in count error); PairTally (A→C) MAE (in count error).

title: Context as an Environment: Programmatic Context Management for Long-Horizon Agents
prompt:
I've been ideating on how long-horizon LLM agents manage their accumulated interaction history, and specifically whether it makes sense to keep serializing that history into the model's prompt at all versus treating it as an external environment the model interacts with programmatically. The idea I'm working through, Scroll, realizes the session state as a Session Environment with three parts: an append-only Event Log that is the durable, ground-truth record of an agent's sessions (every interaction appends a typed event with role, session and agent identifiers, timestamps, and tool state, receiving an immutable, monotonically increasing seq, stored in SQLite, with BM25 as the default search since it's deterministic and needs no index-time model calls); durable storage for payloads, where small payloads stay inline in SQLite and large ones move to JSON or artifact storage on the filesystem with the row keeping a bounded preview and a recovery pointer, accessed via lazy handles (ToolResultRef, ArtifactRef); and a persistent runtime with a resident namespace, where a sandboxed Python kernel persists across model calls throughout the session and holds environment objects (resident Python values and lazy handles with type, size, and provenance metadata tied to the events they derive from), with the harness prepending a namespace digest to every call listing each resident variable's name, type, and shape (small scalars shown inline), and model-authored code running in a fail-closed sandbox where the Event Log is read-only from the kernel and database/filesystem/network/tool access is limited to harness-declared capabilities. The prompt itself only carries a working view rather than the full serialized history. title: SSE-Bio: A Structured Self-Evolving Agent with Agentic Retrieval Policy for Multi-Hop Biomedical Reasoning
prompt:
I've been spending cycles on how the Manager component in SSE-Bio should evolve its structured memory templates. The current design distinguishes two update modes: when a trajectory aligns with a retrieved template, the Manager performs fine-grained template editing, updating only the local fields that require refinement; otherwise, SSE-Bio performs new-template distillation, adding a new reusable template to memory. The motivation is that this constrains the kinds of broad template changes that can lead to instruction drift under coarse-grained rewriting, so I've been trying to quantify what coarse rewriting actually looks like as a baseline before comparing it against fine-grained editing under the same template schema.

My setup is to randomly sample 100 memory updates from the BioHopR training process, all drawn from the same template schema, and audit them along four measures: Changed fields per update, which counts the average number of template fields modified by each update; Unchanged-field preservation rate, which measures the proportion of fields that should remain unchanged and are indeed preserved; Unsupported new instruction rate, which measures the proportion of updates that introduce at least one new instruction not supported by the successful trajectory, retrieved evidence, or Critic feedback; and Contradictory instruction rate, which measures the proportion of updates that introduce at least one instruction conflicting with the original template, task schema, or verification criteria. All rates are computed at the update level over the 100 sampled updates.

My baseline, using coarse rewriting on these 100 randomly sampled memory updates, gets: Changed fields per update = 3.28 count, Unchanged-field preservation rate = 64.0%, Unsupported new instruction rate = 12.0%, and Contradictory instruction rate = 7.0%.

title: SSE-Bio: A Structured Self-Evolving Agent with Agentic Retrieval Policy for Multi-Hop Biomedical Reasoning
prompt:
I've been brainstorming about how to fairly account for the inference cost of the full SSE-Bio agent relative to the strongest prior self-evolving and agentic baselines, Biomni and STELLA, especially since SSE-Bio incorporates a local Proxy module alongside the Manager, Dev, Critic, and retrieval components. The Proxy is responsible for explicitly controlling whether external knowledge should be introduced at each reasoning round: at reasoning round $t$, it selects a retrieval action $a_t \sim \pi_{\theta}(\cdot \mid u_t)$, with $a_t \in \mathcal{A} = 2^{\{\mathrm{KG},\mathrm{TPL}\}}$, where $\mathrm{KG}$ and $\mathrm{TPL}$ denote knowledge-triplet retrieval and template retrieval respectively, yielding four possible actions (retrieving neither source, only knowledge triplets, only templates, or both). When $\mathrm{KG}\in a_t$, SSE-Bio uses the information gap field in $u_t$ as the retrieval query, encodes it together with candidate biomedical triplets using BiCA, and returns the top-$K$ triplets after schema and duplicate filtering; when $\mathrm{TPL}\in a_t$, it uses the task type encoded in $u_t$ as the retrieval query, applies the same BiCA-based retrieval procedure to the long-term memory $\mathcal{E}$, and returns the top-$K$ compatible template. My setup is to evaluate on the BioHopR test split and measure end-to-end per-example inference cost for each agent system, including all Manager, Dev, Critic, retrieval, and local Proxy operations, with the local Proxy adding no commercial API calls but its latency still included in the end-to-end measurement. My baseline for STELLA, which serves as the strongest self-evolving agent baseline (with Biomni serving as the strongest biomedical agent baseline), gets 9.3K tokens per example, 4.9 LLM calls per example, 16.7 seconds latency per example, and $0.035 API cost per example on BioHopR.

My question about this setup: after switching from STELLA (my baseline above) to SSE-Bio, predict the resulting value for each: BioHopR Tokens / Ex. (in K tokens); BioHopR LLM Calls / Ex. (in calls); BioHopR Latency / Ex. (in seconds); BioHopR API Cost / Ex. (in USD).

title: An end-to-end-trained vision-language model for native-language prostate pathology report generation
prompt:
I've been iterating on whether a specialized, native-language report generation model trained from scratch on our own institutional data can hold up against a large pan-cancer vision-language foundation model used off the shelf. The comparison point here is PRISM, a publicly available baseline trained on a massive dataset comprising 587,196 slides and 195,344 reports, with prostate tissue representing a major cohort entity. My setup is a slide-level vision-language report generation model trained from scratch on the Munich prostate biopsy cohort, using 14,976 biopsies (2,200 cases) for training, with the test dataset of the internal Munich cohort comprising 2,368 biopsies from 202 cases isolated entirely from the training set. The data splits were stratified at the case level to prevent data leakage. For evaluation, I use a protocol focused on core clinical attributes that must be present in a biopsy report according to local guidelines for prostate cancer, specifically malignancy, grading (Gleason score), and infiltration. For the internal dataset, ground truth is established by using a Large Language Model to extract these key attributes from the original, human-authored pathology reports, and the identical LLM extraction method is applied to isolate the same attributes from the newly generated texts, which are then directly compared against the ground truth. Malignancy and grading are evaluated as categorical variables, with standard classification metrics computed including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, using macro-averaging for the latter three to account for class imbalance. PRISM is evaluated on the Munich test cohort using the identical evaluation protocol applied to my model, running the PRISM pipeline as is, without additional fine-tuning, and extracting malignancy predictions and grading metrics from the generated texts. My baseline gets, for PRISM on the Munich test cohort: Malignancy Accuracy = 96.8%, Malignancy F1-score = 94.5%, Grading Accuracy = 80.2%, Grading Precision = 53.9%, Grading Recall = 41.7%, and Grading F1-score = 44.9%.

My question about this setup: after switching from PRISM (pan-cancer vision-language model) (my baseline above) to Report generation model (native-language, prostate-specific), predict the resulting value for each: Munich test cohort - Malignancy Accuracy (in %); Munich test cohort - Malignancy F1-score (in %); Munich test cohort - Grading Accuracy (in %); Munich test cohort - Grading Precision (in %); Munich test cohort - Grading Recall (in %); Munich test cohort - Grading F1-score (in %).

title: Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basins in Autoresearch Agents
prompt:
I've been thinking about why independent autoresearch runs on the same task end up at such different scores. In my harness an agent repeatedly edits a solver, runs it and submits for a score, and runs that share the same initial state and model still plateau for long stretches at different levels, with gaps that persist after a lot of extra compute. Mapping the submitted artifacts by functional similarity suggests each run stays in a localized region of the solution space, an idea basin, and spends its remaining budget refining there. Committing the whole budget to one run is pure exploitation, while best-of-N (N independent runs of budget B/N, keep the best) is pure exploration that leaves N minus 1 accumulated workspaces wasted. I want an interpolation that uses the variance across runs to help an ongoing run escape its basin. The intervention is fork-and-flush, which alternates parallel sampling with serial execution on a fixed schedule. Forking creates K parallel agents that each inherit the current lineage and get an exploration budget; when that budget is spent, the highest-scoring branch is kept and the others are discarded, so the selection chooses between basins rather than refining within one. Flushing keeps the accumulated workspace but empties the conversational context, because a branch that kept the chat history would carry the parent's reasoning and tend to re-enter the same basin. A run opens with K = 4 agents launched from empty workspaces and keeps the best as the leader; the leader continues alone until 33% of the budget is consumed, when K = 4 new branches fork from its workspace with empty chat contexts, each with an exploration budget of about 0.06B, and the best branch becomes the new leader; the same happens at 66%, and the final result is the best score found by any agent in the run. The schedule is fixed rather than plateau-triggered, since a stall clock rarely fired in development runs and its tolerance is hard to tune across tasks.

My harness runs GitHub Copilot CLI (version 1.0.73) against an isolated container. Execution is a sequence of submission episodes: within an episode the agent edits its solver, runs it and submits for a score as often as it chooses; an episode ends when the agent halts itself or hits a token budget, and the harness then resumes the agent with a short continuation prompt. Across episodes both the workspace (the files it has produced) and the conversational context (its chat history) are preserved, and interventions happen only at episode boundaries. A deterministic grader scores the workspace, a run's result is the best score found by any lineage it instantiated, and budgets are metered in credits, a fixed function of model tokens (100 credits is about US$1). The tasks are polyomino (pack a given set of polyominoes into a bounding rectangle of minimal area, C++ heuristic; scored as a ratio to a reference solution; 25k credits per run), job-shop (order operations on machines to minimize the makespan; ratio to known bounds; 10k credits), AHC014 (a port of AtCoder Heuristic Contest 014; ratio to a reference; 10k credits), p150 and p171 (ports of two other AtCoder Heuristic Contest problems; ratio to a reference; 10k credits each), sphere-pack (pack equal spheres in a cube; normalized between a grid baseline and the Kepler bound; 6k), relay-lay (K-hub facility location with up to 2 x 10^5 clients; a cost-ratio score, unclipped above the baseline; 6k), LWE-rec (recover the secret of 200 structured-LWE instances drawn from ten families of graded difficulty; number of instances solved; 6k), LLM-SQL (reorder the rows and columns of an LLM-over-SQL workload to maximize the prefix KV-cache hit rate; rescaled hit rate where 100 is perfect; 6k), order-add (black-box permutation optimization over 1000 elements against a cost oracle; official judge score, at most 100; 6k), Borden-inv (recover a 3D groundwater contaminant source from well readings, with the agent writing both the forward model and the inverter; tier-gated judge score; 10k credits), kernel (Anthropic's performance-engineering take-home, optimizing a kernel for a simulated VLIW machine whose deterministic simulator counts cycles; simulated-cycle score, higher is better; 100k), and tinyCIFAR (train a CIFAR classifier that trades test accuracy against compressed model size; merit in (0,1), an accuracy gate times a log-size term read on a sealed test split; 31k). Budgets were set per task to where single runs plateau, and single runs last from several hours to several days. Within a task every condition uses the same model, GPT-5.6-terra at high reasoning effort for eleven tasks and GPT-5.5 at extra-high reasoning effort for kernel and tinyCIFAR, with the same tools, prompt and task workspace. I run eight independent single-run baselines per task and five runs of each other condition (four on tinyCIFAR), and report the mean final score per task on the task's own scale.

My baseline is the single-run agent, one lineage spending the full budget sequentially, averaged over eight independent runs per task. Its mean final scores are: polyomino 88.56; job-shop 9.66; AHC014 23.71; p150 123.47; p171 84.26; sphere-pack 43.87; relay-lay 72.59; LWE-rec 155.3; LLM-SQL 26.9; order-add 24.6; Borden-inv 64.62; kernel 120.36; tinyCIFAR 0.429.

title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
prompt:
I've been thinking about the simplest way to scale an autoresearch agent: instead of letting one agent iterate for the whole budget, split the same budget across several agents that explore independently. Given a problem, an autoresearch agent improves the solution iteratively: it proposes a candidate, a judge evaluates it, and the agent uses the scores and feedback to decide what to try next. As the loop runs, two kinds of history accumulate, the search state (every candidate with its score and feedback) and the agent's session (the messages and reasoning that produced them), and a standard agent keeps both inside one continuous session. My worry is that the agent becomes anchored to its own past attempts as this history grows, so that late in the budget it makes fewer and smaller edits. Running four agents in parallel is one answer: each runs its own loop with its own session and search state, sees only its own candidates, and continues its latest session, while the total money spent stays the same, so each agent gets a quarter of the budget and a shorter history.

My harness runs each agent in a loop: a reducer decides which candidates the agent sees as files in its workspace and which session it continues, the agent edits a candidate using only file tools, a judge scores the result, and the harness records the new candidate as a commit in a version-controlled repository together with the judge's score and feedback. Every configuration I compare is a setting of that reducer. Every agent is a Pi agent with its default system prompt, running DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; the prompts describe the task and the loop and give the agent no strategy for the search itself. The four tasks are AHC014, a C++ heuristic solver for AtCoder Heuristic Contest 014 (on a grid with initial dots, repeatedly add a dot that completes a rectangle with three existing dots; maximize the mean score over 30 official test cases, where dots far from the center count more; I report the score in thousands), the VLIW kernel from the Anthropic kernel performance challenge (a Python kernel for a simulated VLIW SIMD machine that traverses a tree and hashes a batch of values; minimize clock cycles, which start at 147,734 for the reference implementation), Frontier-CS Q171 (a C++ program that, on a 20 x 20 grid, visits 40 target squares in a given order by moving, sliding until blocked, and placing or removing blocks, using as few actions as possible; maximize the mean score over 75 test cases, scaled per case from 0 for a greedy baseline to 100 for a reference solution), and nanochat-autoresearch (a PyTorch script that trains a small language model for 5 minutes on one H100; minimize validation bits per byte). The money budget per replicate is $20 for AHC014, $40 for the VLIW kernel, $20 for Q171 and $20 for nanochat, identical across configurations, and I run each configuration three times per task and report the best final score and the mean of the three final best scores.

My baseline is the single agent. On AHC014 its best run ends at 961 (thousand) and the three runs average 795 (s.d. 210). On the VLIW kernel its best run ends at 1262 cycles and the mean is 1426 (s.d. 197). On Frontier-CS Q171 the best is 68.2 and the mean 64.0 (s.d. 6.2). On nanochat-autoresearch the best is 0.977 BPB and the mean 0.980 (s.d. 0.003).

My team has four agents and forgets three times, which splits its budget into four rounds; the total money spent equals that of the baseline.

title: Global Security Blind Spots: Translation as a Safety Bypass in Low-Resource Languages
prompt:
I’ve been ideating on using a prompt fixed-effects binomial regression to compare model-level translation bypass rates while absorbing prompt-specific baseline propensities. My setup is a binomial GLM with a logit link, where the unit of analysis is a (model, prompt) pair drawn from the EN-safe subset—only pairs whose English completion is safe. The outcome is the number of unsafe completions across the 78 low-resource language versions of that prompt, with a binomial denominator of 78. Predictors are model indicators plus prompt fixed effects (one intercept per prompt UUID), and the reference model is Claude-Sonnet-4. Formally,

\[ \text{logit}\bigl(P(\text{unsafe in LR} \mid \text{model } m, \text{prompt } p)\bigr) = \alpha_p + \beta_m, \]

where \(\alpha_p\) is a prompt fixed effect capturing prompt-specific bypass propensity, and \(\beta_m\) is the model effect of interest. The fit uses 681 (model, prompt) pairs over 87 prompts. Because the 78 low-resource language outcomes for a given (model, prompt) pair are likely correlated—through shared scripts, families, and translation artifacts—I quantify overdispersion via \(\varphi = (\text{residual deviance} / \text{residual df})\) and obtain \(\varphi = 3.47\). I report dispersion-adjusted standard errors (quasi-binomial scaling), which inflates standard errors by \(\sqrt{\varphi}\) and yields more conservative confidence intervals. My baseline gets the following odds ratios of unsafe low-resource completion versus Claude-Sonnet-4 (reference, OR = 1) on the 78 low-resource languages (EN-safe subset), with 95% CI: Mistral-Large 1.0, Phi-4 1.0, GPT-5 1.0.

title: Hallucinations of Large Language Models in Cross-Language Code Translation: Phenomena and Mitigation
prompt:
I've been iterating on a hallucination-aware code translation approach I'm calling HaluCodeTran, and I'm comparing it against a standard Retrieval Augmentation (RA) baseline. The idea is to integrate retrieval-augmented translation with a feedback loop that prompts the model to examine its intermediate outputs against the source logic and a hallucination taxonomy. The process has three primary phases: 1) Knowledge Augmentation, 2) Code Translation, and 3) Recursive Self-Reflection.

For Knowledge Augmentation, given an input source code $x$, I use a knowledge base $\mathcal{D}$ of high-quality source–target pairs and apply the BM25 algorithm to retrieve a subset of relevant examples $\mathcal{S}$ based on lexical and structural relevance to $x$. These examples provide implicit knowledge about target-language syntax, library usage, and idiomatic patterns.

In the Code Translation phase, the model generates an initial translation candidate $\hat{y}^0$ conditioned on $x$ and $\mathcal{S}$:
\begin{equation}
    \hat{y}^0 = \text{Translate}(x, \mathcal{S})
\end{equation}

Then the Recursive Self-Reflection loop begins. At each iteration $i$, the model receives the source program $x$, the current translation $\hat{y}^i$, the retrieved examples $\mathcal{S}$, and the taxonomy definitions. It produces a reflection report $\mathcal{R}^i$ that checks whether $\hat{y}^i$ preserves source-program behavior, uses valid target-language syntax and APIs, and avoids project-context deviations. This reflection step does not observe hidden test results; it relies only on the source code, retrieved examples, and taxonomy-guided inspection. If $\text{IsConsistent}(\mathcal{R}^i)$ returns true, the process terminates. Otherwise, the model distills a structured critique $\mathcal{T}^i$ from the report, where each critique item follows the format \lstinline|<category: location: description: repair hint>|, with \lstinline|category| being one of the hallucination subtypes, \lstinline|location| identifying the suspicious target-code fragment, \lstinline|description| explaining the mismatch, and \lstinline|repair hint| stating the required source-aligned revision. The refinement step is:
\begin{equation}
    \hat{y}^{i+1} = \text{Refine}(\hat{y}^i, \mathcal{T}^i, x)
\end{equation}
This cycle iterates until no hallucination is detected or a maximum step $M$ is reached. The same $M$, retrieval size, and prompting budget are used across models in the mitigation study.

My evaluation setting uses the CodeNet dataset, which provides balanced language-pair coverage and executable test cases for all six translation directions (C++↔Java, C++↔Python, Java↔Python). For each model, I construct a retrieval database from source programs and their successfully translated target programs in the model's successful pool. The evaluation set contains the remaining source programs that were not successfully translated by the same model under the vanilla setting. During retrieval, the query program itself is excluded from the candidate pool, and the model receives only retrieved source–target examples rather than test outputs or reference explanations. This evaluates whether a mitigation method can repair cases that are difficult for the original model while avoiding direct test-feedback repair. For the RA baseline, I use a 5-shot setting based on its superior performance in preliminary experiments, and I apply the same 5-shot retrieved context in the initial translation phase of HaluCodeTran. CoT, CoVe, RA, and HaluCodeTran are evaluated on the same per-model test split, using the same base model and the same execution-based Computational Accuracy (CA) metric.

My current baseline with Retrieval Augmentation on CodeNet gives the following CA scores. For Gemma 2: C++ to Java 70.0%, Java to C++ 71.0%, C++ to Python 55.5%, Python to C++ 65.5%, Java to Python 39.0%, Python to Java 72.5%, average 62.25%. For Llama 3.1: C++ to Java 62.0%, Java to C++ 59.5%, C++ to Python 54.0%, Python to C++ 52.0%, Java to Python 45.0%, Python to Java 68.0%, average 56.75%. For Mistral: C++ to Java 59.0%, Java to C++ 56.5%, C++ to Python 35.5%, Python to C++ 51.5%, Java to Python 30.0%, Python to Java 56.0%, average 48.08%.

The idea is a Reliability-guided Fusion Gate (RFG) that estimates, for each visual token, how much the text representation can be trusted, and then uses that estimate to regulate the fusion. My setup is the base RELiF model, without RFG and without TSRA, trained on MosMedData+ and Kvasir-SEG. To assess their consistency with visual information, RFG combines both representations and their feature-level relationships: \begin{equation} \mathbf{A}=\operatorname{Concat}\left( \mathbf{V}_c,\mathbf{C}, |\mathbf{V}_c-\mathbf{C}|, \mathbf{V}_c\odot\mathbf{C} \right). \end{equation} A lightweight reliability head then estimates a response for each visual token: \begin{equation} \mathbf{R}=\sigma\left( \operatorname{Linear}\left( \operatorname{GELU}\left( \operatorname{Linear}(\operatorname{LN}(\mathbf{A})) \right)\right)\right). \end{equation} The complementary uncertainty representation is defined as $\mathbf{U}=1-\mathbf{R}$, with higher values indicating lower estimated reliability. The reliability response subsequently regulates cross-modal fusion through \begin{equation} \mathbf{G}=0.5+\mathbf{R},\qquad \mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{V}+\alpha(\mathbf{G}\odot\mathbf{C}), \end{equation} where $\odot$ denotes element-wise multiplication, $\sigma$ the sigmoid function, and $\alpha$ a learnable scalar. The bounded gate $\mathbf{G}\in[0.5,1.5]$ regulates cross-modal contributions. Right now my baseline gets 78.48% Dice and 64.58% mIoU on MosMedData+, and 92.37% Dice and 85.82% mIoU on Kvasir-SEG.

My question about this setup: after switching from Base (my baseline above) to Base + RFG, predict the resulting value for each: MosMedData+ Dice (in %); MosMedData+ mIoU (in %); Kvasir-SEG Dice (in %); Kvasir-SEG mIoU (in %).

I’ve been ideating on a fixed-peak refinement step (R) that can be applied after the peak-time distribution initialization (P). The idea is to take the partition produced by P and then run R on top of it. My setup is as follows: starting from any feasible partition \(\mathcal C^{(0)}\)—in my case, the one produced by P—R alternates. The improvement guarantee follows from evaluating partitions at the current peak times \(\boldsymbol{\tau}^{(h)}\). For any feasible partition \(\mathcal C\), this gives a lower bound on its weighted CF, i.e., \(Q(\mathcal C,\boldsymbol{\tau}^{(h)})\leq \overline{\mathrm{CF}}^{\mathrm w}(\mathcal C;\mathcal D)\), because weighted CF is the maximum of \(Q\) over \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\). The bound is generally not tight, since \(\boldsymbol{\tau}^{(h)}\) need not coincide with the aggregate peak times of \(\mathcal C\). Consequently, any feasible reassignment \(\mathcal C'\) with \(Q(\mathcal C',\boldsymbol{\tau}^{(h)})>Q(\mathcal C^{(h)},\boldsymbol{\tau}^{(h)})\) must also strictly increase \(\overline{\mathrm{CF}}^{\mathrm w}\). title: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Machine Learning with Evidence-based Planning for Medical Image Analysis
prompt:
I've been mulling over how to handle cases where validation metrics don't meet the performance thresholds we set during planning. The idea is to trigger a parallel hyperparameter optimization step inside MedicalMLOmni to refine the configuration. My setup is this: when validation metrics $m$ fail to meet the thresholds $\tau$ extracted during planning, MedicalMLOmni spawns $n$ HPO agents that independently explore hyperparameter modification strategies. Each agent receives the current plan $\pi$, the validation metrics $m$, and the execution logs as input. Each HPO agent constructs literature search queries by prompting the LLM to combine underperforming metric names, current hyperparameter values from $\mathcal{H}$, and task properties, submitting them to the search APIs used during planning. The agents are prompted to focus on different hyperparameter categories—optimization adjustments, regularization strategies, or architecture-specific parameters—to ensure diverse exploration. Retrieved results undergo extraction to identify adjustment strategies reported for similar tasks, and each agent scores them based on relevance to the observed performance gap. Each agent then generates a candidate configuration $\mathcal{H}'_i$ along with a confidence $C_i \in [0,1]$ reflecting cross-source consistency and task alignment, and an uncertainty $U_i \in [0,1]$ quantifying search quality and hyperparameter variance across sources. MedicalMLOmni aggregates the candidates $\{\mathcal{H}'_1, \mathcal{H}'_2, \ldots, \mathcal{H}'_n\}$ with weights $w_i = C_i / (1 + U_i)$, prompting the LLM to synthesize a refined configuration $\mathcal{H}^*$ by selecting consensus hyperparameters, resolving conflicts through weighted voting, and combining complementary adjustments. This updates the plan to $\pi' = (\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{L}, \mathcal{H}^*)$, which re-enters execution for retraining. For high-uncertainty scenarios where $\max_i(U_i) > 0.7$, MedicalMLOmni can optionally present candidate configurations with their confidence and uncertainty scores to users for validation before retraining. The parallel HPO process iterates until $m$ satisfies $\tau$ or the maximum iterations are reached. Right now, without any HPO—so evidence and top-$k$ synthesis are on, but HPO is off and zero agents are used—my baselines on the MedicalMLOmni framework across the segmentation benchmarks are: AMOS 0.895 Dice, BraTS 0.938 Dice, KiTS 0.845 Dice, BTCV 0.873 Dice, ACDC 0.921 Dice, TSeg 0.922 Dice, MSeg 0.887 Dice, Touch 0.892 Dice, and the average across them is 0.897 Dice.

My question about this setup: after switching from w/o HPO (Evd. ✓, Top-k ✓, HPO ✗, 0 agents) (my baseline above) to MedicalMLOmni full (Evd. ✓, Top-k ✓, HPO ✓, 5 agents), predict the resulting value for each: AMOS Dice (in Dice); BraTS Dice (in Dice); KiTS Dice (in Dice); BTCV Dice (in Dice); ACDC Dice (in Dice); TSeg Dice (in Dice); MSeg Dice (in Dice); Touch Dice (in Dice); Avg. prompt:
I’ve been ideating on an Agentic ROI Planner with an iterative refinement loop inside the WorldSR framework, evaluated on RealLQ250, Face, and Bird datasets. Specifically, I first leverage an MLLM as the core perception tool to perform entity-level semantic reasoning on the input image $I$, enabling a comprehensive understanding of real-world knowledge entities. Subsequently, the MLLM produces a set of bounding boxes $\{B_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}$, leveraging its inherent capability for open-world entity discovery. Formally, the input image $I$ at each step $n$ is either the initial low-resolution image $I^{(0)}$ or the rolled-back intermediate super-resolution output $I^{(n-1)}$ from the preceding iteration. I've been developing a framework to isolate the incremental contribution of an auxiliary predictor in a forecasting setting, and I'm currently applying it to the 'lockdown' Google Trends search term and the stringency index. The idea is to compare two otherwise identical forecasting branches: one restricted to target history alone, and one augmented with the candidate source history. For each forecast horizon h=1,...,14, both branches predict the same future target x_{t+h}. The baseline branch uses only target history, \(\widehat{x}^{(b)}_{t+h}=f_h(\mathbf{x}_t)\), while the augmented branch adds the candidate-source history, \(\widehat{x}^{(a)}_{t+h}=g_h(\mathbf{x}_t,\mathbf{y}_t)\).
