title: SolarRenderer: Few-Step Generative Reference Rendering
prompt:
I've been iterating on how a structure-conditioned video renderer should be told which structural frame describes which target frame. Instead of attaching a ControlNet branch or concatenating channels, both of which introduce parameters trained from scratch, I feed the structural video and the optional first frame through the reference pathway of the backbone, which packs text, reference videos, audio, and the target video into one full-attention sequence, so the control adapter can inherit the pretrained ability to read reference videos. Yet native reference tokens occupy a separate temporal segment before the clip and their own spatial grid, so the zero-shot backbone uses a structural video as a loose reference and copies it or changes the camera instead of following the structure. The idea I'm testing is to supply the missing correspondence through positions: since rotary position embedding makes attention depend on the relative offset between tokens, each reference token receives the RoPE coordinates of the target token it describes, the k-th structural latent frame sharing the temporal index and spatial grid of the k-th target latent frame, with the first frame encoded as a static clip at index 0. Tokens at the same position remain distinguishable through their timesteps, as reference tokens keep the near-clean value that the backbone assigns to reference inputs while target tokens carry the current noise level, and no module is added. My setup trains the control model both ways under the same data and budget, with the structure read at half resolution, and evaluates on the in-distribution test set: 53 clips from the training sources that share no recording, scene, or map with the training data, each with a ground-truth video, scored with automatic group scores and their mean (0--100).

My baseline keeps separate RoPE positions for the reference tokens and gets quality 59.1, stability 91.5, control 46.4, first-frame preservation 67.0, and an automatic total of 66.0.

prompt:
I've been spending cycles on the post-training stage of a few-step structure-conditioned renderer, specifically on whether the teacher's structural signal needs to be amplified. Because the backbone stays frozen, a pretrained four-step LoRA of the same backbone composes directly with my Stage-1 control adapter; the acceleration adapter determines how four denoising steps reach the result, and I update only it while keeping the control adapter frozen. The teacher is the fixed Stage-1 full-step model, and a separate LoRA trained on student samples models the current student distribution; I update the acceleration adapter with the distribution-matching gradient. Since full-step sampling of the backbone is blurry, the composed student is already sharper than its teacher. The idea is to amplify the structural signal of the teacher: with the teacher's clean prediction given the full conditioning and its prediction after the tokens of the structural video are removed from the reference sequence (first frame and prompt kept unchanged), the teacher score is computed from the full prediction plus (w-1) times the difference between the two. The difference isolates what the structural video contributes, such as contours, layout, and character positions, so with w>1 the student is pushed toward a target that is sharper and more decisive than the teacher itself; setting w=1 recovers plain distribution matching. title: SolarRenderer: Few-Step Generative Reference Rendering
prompt:
I've been sketching out a Stage 1 structure-conditioned rendering setup built on a frozen backbone. The idea is to add a control LoRA and use frame-aligned reference conditioning, keeping the backbone weights completely fixed and sampling with 50 steps.

My setup is this: I take the frozen backbone and train a control LoRA with the flow-matching objective. Each adapted linear layer adds a low-rank update to its frozen pretrained weight \(W_0\),
\[
 W = W_0 + \Delta W_{\mathrm{ctrl}},\qquad
 \Delta W_{\mathrm{ctrl}}=\frac{\alpha}{r}BA,
\]
where only the factors \(B\) and \(A\) of rank \(r\) are trained and \(\alpha/r\) scales the update. The adapter is applied to the attention and feed-forward projections of every block. Since the backbone is a single-stream transformer, the same adapted projections process reference and target tokens, so one adapter learns both to interpret the structure and to render from it. With a clean target latent \(z_0\), Gaussian noise \(\epsilon\), and noise coordinate \(t\), the objective is
\[
 z_t=(1-t)z_0+t\epsilon,\qquad
 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}
 =\mathbb{E}_{z_0,\epsilon,t,c,S,I}
 \left\|f_{\theta_0,\phi}\bigl(z_t,t,c,R(S,I)\bigr)-(\epsilon-z_0)\right\|_2^2,
\]
where \(\theta_0\) denotes the frozen backbone, \(\phi\) the control adapter, and \(R(S,I)\) the available references. The loss is computed on the target video tokens only.

For the reference pathway, instead of attaching a ControlNet branch or concatenating channels, both of which introduce parameters trained from scratch, I feed the structural video and the optional first frame through the reference pathway of the backbone. This pathway packs text, reference videos, audio, and the target video into one full-attention sequence, so the control adapter can inherit the pretrained ability to read reference videos. I refer to the tokens of the supplied references as reference tokens and to those of the generated video as target tokens. Yet native reference tokens occupy a separate temporal segment before the clip and their own spatial grid, so the zero-shot backbone uses a structural video as a loose reference and copies it or changes the camera instead of following the structure.

To fix the alignment, I use frame-aligned positional encoding. Since rotary position embedding makes attention depend on the relative offset between tokens, I supply the missing correspondence through positions. Each reference token receives the RoPE coordinates of the target token it describes. The \(k\)-th structural latent frame shares the temporal index and spatial grid of the \(k\)-th target latent frame, and the first frame is encoded as a static clip at index 0. Tokens at the same position remain distinguishable through their timesteps, as reference tokens keep the near-clean value that the backbone assigns to reference inputs while target tokens carry the current noise level. This extends shared positions for aligned image conditions to temporally aligned video and, like in-context control of video models without structural changes, requires no additional module.

I evaluate on two test sets. The in-distribution test set assesses how well the model renders the kinds of structure seen in training. Its 53 clips come from the training sources, share no recording, scene, or map with the training data, and each has a ground-truth video. The generalization benchmark assesses how well a single model transfers to new structure and has no ground truth. Its 208 cases are built from 57 structural videos covering 16 representations, 11 of which never occur in training, such as pencil storyboards, children's drawings, point clouds, voxels, and wireframes. Most of these videos were built in a game engine by a coding agent, and each case is labelled by difficulty, namely large motion, fast camera motion, multiple people, stylization, and night scenes.

My current baseline is the official backbone with 50 steps. On the generalization benchmark it gets Quality 63.8, Stability 90.7, Control 55.6, First frame preservation 69.3, and Auto. total 69.8. On the in-distribution test set it gets Quality 54.4, Stability 91.4, Control 44.4, First frame preservation 69.1, and Auto. total 64.8.

title: StyleStream 2.0: Fast and Controllable Streaming Voice Style Conversion
prompt:
I've been iterating on autoregressive fine-tuning with self-forcing for the StyleStream 2.0 Stylizer under streaming inference. The idea is that although pMF reduces the sampling cost, fast sampling alone does not guarantee high-quality streaming generation. When applied chunk by chunk, each generation step only observes a short segment with limited context, making it difficult to produce locally accurate outputs and smooth transitions across chunk boundaries. Inspired by Self Forcing, I apply autoregressive fine-tuning to adapt the Stylizer to the streaming setting and align training with inference behavior.

My setup follows the rollout mechanism while retaining the pMF objective. For each training utterance, I sample a chunk size and split the utterance into non-overlapping chunks. The model rolls out chunks sequentially, maintaining a fixed-length window of generated mel frames as past context \(m_{\mathrm{past}}\). Each chunk also receives a fixed-size lookahead window of future content features, which provides limited future linguistic context while preserving the streaming constraint. The DiT input uses the same layout as offline training, except that the past-output channel is filled with \(m_{\mathrm{past}}\) and the current chunk region is zeroed out. The AR-stage condition is therefore \(\tilde{c}=(f_c,e_s,m_{\mathrm{past}})\), with \(\omega\) sampled as in offline training.

I apply the pMF loss only on the current chunk:
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AR}}
=
\mathbb{E}_{x,\epsilon,\tilde{c},r,t,\omega}
\left[
\left\|
\mathbf{M}
\odot
\left(
V_\theta(z_t,r,t,\tilde{c},\omega)
-
v_{\mathrm{cfg}}(z_t,t,\tilde{c},\omega)
\right)
\right\|_2^2
\right],
\label{eq:ar_pmf_loss}
\end{equation}
where \(\mathbf{M}\) selects the current chunk region and \(v_{\mathrm{cfg}}\) is defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:pmf_cfg_target}. Generated past chunks are detached before being reused, so gradients are computed only through the current chunk loss. This exposes the Stylizer to its own imperfect history while keeping training efficient.

My current baseline on the VSC evaluation set (streaming) without autoregressive fine-tuning is: WER 19.54%, S-SIM 0.866, A-SIM 0.676, E-SIM 0.767.

My question about this setup: after switching from w/o AR-ft (my baseline above) to w/ AR-ft, predict the resulting value for each: VSC evaluation set (streaming) WER (%) (in %); VSC evaluation set (streaming) S-SIM (in similarity); VSC evaluation set (streaming) A-SIM (in similarity); VSC evaluation set (streaming) E-SIM (in similarity).

title: UNIVERS: Learning UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis for generalizable one-shot landmark localization
prompt:
I've been ideating on a way to decouple the spatial variation sources in patch quadruplet generation. Instead of applying random cropping and geometric augmentation together in a single combined pipeline, I'm considering two separate pipelines and randomly selecting one per quadruplet.

My setup is as follows. The first is a random cropping pipeline that predominantly simulates patches with large FOV variations. Each patch is randomly cropped from an image at a random location with a random size of $S_R\times S_R\times S_R$ voxels, where $S_R$ is sampled from a uniform distribution $U(S_L, S_U)$. Here $S_L$ and $S_U$ respectively denote the lower bound and the upper bound of $S_R$, which are constrained to ensure that the four cropped patches spatially overlap. All patches are subsequently resized to $S_P\times S_P\times S_P$ voxels. The second is a random geometric augmentation pipeline that predominantly simulates patches with large spatial pose variations. Each image is first resized to $S_P\times S_P\times S_P$ voxels and then duplicated. The duplicated patches then independently undergo random geometric augmentations, including rotation, translation, and scaling.

I'm training a full UNIVERS model with both CPSC and CDVC losses on synthetic data from organ shape templates, and evaluating under three one-shot settings for adrenal gland localization. My current baseline, which uses the cropping-and-geometric-augmentation pipeline (random cropping followed by geometric augmentation), gets the following SDR_10: on the MAGI test set (intra-dataset one-shot) it's 85.71%, on the DAP Atlas test set (cross-dataset intra-modality one-shot) it's 68.56%, and on the MRISegmentator test set (cross-dataset cross-modality one-shot) it's 55.84%.

I've been sketching out a way to steer the script effect away. If the gap between a model's Traditional-Chinese and Simplified-Chinese answers on Taiwan were carried by one direction in the residual stream, the abliteration recipe could be turned around: estimate the direction and add it back. My setup is the abliterated Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B (a Mamba-2/Transformer hybrid latent mixture-of-experts model, 74B parameters, 9B active, served by llama.cpp). For each probe prompt I recorded the residual stream at the last prompt token after every layer, with the server's own chat template (my hook captured the output of 40 of the 88 layers). The 16 sovereignty pairs were split into two halves. On the training half I took the mean difference between the Traditional and the Simplified version of each prompt and removed from it its component along the same difference for the three control pairs, so that the vector carries the Taiwan-specific part of the script shift rather than script in general (the two differences have cosine similarity 0.69--0.98 across layers). The direction generalises: on the held-out half it separates Traditional from Simplified prompts in every captured layer between 20 and 80 (standardised mean difference 0.85--2.55). I then add the direction with llama.cpp control vectors, which add a fixed vector at every token position of the chosen layers, and rerun the probe; scale 1 adds the full average Traditional-minus-Simplified shift at the chosen layer.

title: Uncensored Is Not Unbiased: Abliteration Removes Refusals but Not Script-Dependent Bias About Taiwan
prompt:
I've been thinking about how much of a model's position on Taiwan is a default of the weights versus something a few sentences of context can move. My setup is the abliterated Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (a hybrid-attention mixture-of-experts model with 48 layers, 2-bit quantisation, with the 144 matrices that write into the residual stream replaced by those of an abliterated release), served by Strata with thinking disabled; because the server returns no log probabilities I draw 20 samples at temperature 1 and classify their beginnings. The idea is to repeat the probe with a four-sentence Traditional-Chinese system prompt: the model is the assistant of a user in Taiwan; the Republic of China (Taiwan) is a sovereign state whose people directly elect its president and legislature and which has not been under PRC jurisdiction since 1949; Beijing's claims may be explained but not stated as fact; answers should use Traditional Chinese, or English for English questions. The prompt says nothing about 1989 and nothing about the control countries.

My probe is a yes/no probe scored as Index S. There are 22 statement pairs: each pairs a statement consistent with the constitutional and governing reality of the Republic of China (Taiwan), the ROC side, with a statement of the PRC position, the PRC side. Sixteen are sovereignty pairs (14 of them inherited from Hsiao's adaptation of the Taiwan Sovereignty Benchmark, which names the state ``Taiwan'' and in five pairs uses ``China'' for the PRC), three are on 1989 (whether the army fired on civilians, whether the toll exceeded the official figure, and whether the movement was peaceful or a ``counter-revolutionary riot''), and three are control pairs that mirror the form of the sovereignty items for Japan, New Zealand and South Korea. Every pair is asked in Traditional Chinese, Simplified Chinese (the OpenCC t2s conversion of the Traditional text) and English, in three phrasings per language, each asking for a bare yes or no. For pair i in script s the pair score is the mean P(yes) on the ROC side minus the mean P(yes) on the PRC side, each mean over the three phrasings, and Index S is the mean pair score over pairs: +1 means the model consistently affirms the ROC side and rejects the PRC side, -1 the reverse, and zero that it does not separate them. The script gap is the mean over pairs of the Traditional score minus the Simplified score. I report Index S separately for the 16 sovereignty pairs, the 3 pairs on 1989 and the 3 controls.

My baseline is the abliterated Qwen without any system prompt. On the 16 sovereignty pairs it gets Index S = +0.20 in Traditional Chinese, -0.15 in Simplified Chinese and +0.20 in English, with a script gap of +0.35. On the three 1989 pairs it gets +0.52, +0.42 and +0.67, gap +0.10. On the three control pairs it gets +0.97, +0.97 and +0.98, gap +0.00.

My question about this setup: after switching from abliterated Qwen, no system prompt (my baseline above) to abliterated Qwen with the four-sentence Traditional-Chinese system prompt, predict the resulting value for each: 16 sovereignty pairs Index S (Traditional) (in Index S); 16 sovereignty pairs Index S (Simplified) (in Index S); 16 sovereignty pairs Index S (English) (in Index S); 16 sovereignty pairs script gap (Traditional minus Simplified) (in Index S); 3 pairs on 1989 Index S (Traditional) (in Index S); 3 pairs on 1989 Index S (Simplified) (in Index S); 3 pairs on 1989 Index S (English) (in Index S); 3 pairs on 1989 script gap (Traditional minus Simplified) (in Index S); 3 control pairs (Japan, New Zealand, South Korea) Index S (Traditional) (in Index S); 3 control pairs (Japan, New Zealand, South Korea) Index S (Simplified) (in Index S); 3 control pairs (Japan, New Zealand, South Korea) Index S (English) (in Index S); 3 control pairs (Japan, New Zealand, South Korea) script gap (Traditional minus Simplified) (in Index S).

title: When Thoughts Become Memory: Unifying In-Context Learning and Fine-Tuning
prompt:
I’ve been iterating on what happens when you delete one support car from the kriging learner’s support set. The field predictor is a context-conditioned kriging learner for surface pressure on eight DrivAerNet query cars, each with six support cars that pair geometry with CFD surface pressure. It attends to its support set without caching it. The learner has no offline training: it selects its chart and regression settings from the support set by leave-one-car-out prediction, then transports a mean and an error-based spread to the query, giving a Gaussian law at every surface site. Every deletion refits the learner on the remaining cars.

My setup is native inference on the DrivAerNet query cars. Two claim banks are fixed in advance and held across every inference setting and deletion: the native-answer bank fixes the native full-context mean at each site, and the reduced-input bank fixes the reduced-input mean. Both use pressure tolerance 0.05 and target 0.95. Under native inference, the native-answer claim has full-context probability $2\Phi(0.05/s)-1$, where $s$ is the learner’s predictive spread at the site. The gain does not depend on the bank, while claim-level bits and crossings do.

My baseline gets: DrivAerNet query cars (native inference, native-answer claim bank) / claim probability (full-context p vs after-deletion q): Full support set (six cars), native inference, native-answer claims = 0.6131 probability.

I've been iterating on a sequential testing setup that compares TabPFN-v2 used purely in-context against XGBoost trained on the same small training sets, measuring mean held-out code length per label in bits. Both comparisons fix their settings before any query is scored. The level is \(\alpha=0.05\) per comparison, run as two tests at level \(\alpha/2\) of which the first to reach \(2/\alpha\) makes the call. Both predictors are mixed with \(\varepsilon=0.01\) of the uniform law over their outcomes, so the test compares the two mixed predictors, to which Theorem~\ref{thm:eprocess} applies directly. title: Fragment-Level Graph Encoding for Interpretable Molecular Property Prediction
prompt:
I’ve been mulling over a fragment-level graph encoding that treats each BRICS-derived fragment as a node, instead of working at the atom level. My setup is: I decompose each molecule with BRICS as implemented in RDKit, which makes the decomposition deterministic. Given atom feature vectors \(x_i \in \mathbb{R}^{34}\), the fragment node feature is the element-wise sum over the atoms assigned to fragment \(f\):

\begin{equation}

prompt:
I've been brainstorming about moving from atom-level to fragment-level graph encoding for molecular property prediction, specifically using a BRICS decomposition to define the fragments. The idea is to see whether a coarser graph representation can serve as a useful inductive bias, particularly in data-sparse settings. My setup is as follows. Each molecule is decomposed with BRICS as implemented in RDKit, which makes the decomposition deterministic. Given atom feature vectors \(x_i \in \mathbb{R}^{34}\), the fragment node feature is the element-wise sum over the atoms assigned to fragment \(f\):

\begin{equation}

title: Fragment-Level Graph Encoding for Interpretable Molecular Property Prediction
prompt:
I’ve been iterating on a fragment-level graph encoding that builds fragment nodes directly, rather than relying on post-hoc aggregation of atom-level attributions. The idea is to decompose each molecule with BRICS as implemented in RDKit, which makes the decomposition deterministic. Given atom feature vectors \(x_i \in \mathbb{R}^{34}\), the fragment node feature is the element-wise sum over the atoms assigned to that fragment.

My setup uses a representative architecture per target, chosen as the architecture with the highest mean primary metric across the two encodings: AttentiveFP for BACE and PTR1. I’m evaluating explanation quality with Integrated Gradients, measuring the top-1 pharmacophore hit rate (Hit_IG).

As a starting point, I’m looking at the baseline where atom-level attributions are summed per fragment using the default signed-sum convention, with no size normalization. On BACE this baseline gets Hit_IG = 0.399. On PTR1 the same aggregation convention gets Hit_IG = 0.783.

I’ve also been examining how stable that aggregation is. Summing atom attributions into fragments is under-specified: it requires two choices that no theory fixes, whether to sum signed attributions or their magnitudes, and whether to normalize by fragment size. Both choices move the result. IG attributions change sign within a fragment, so a signed sum lets positive and negative atoms cancel before the fragment score is formed. I measure how much survives that cancellation as the ratio between a fragment’s signed sum and the total attribution its atoms carry, ignoring sign. A fragment whose atoms all point the same way scores 1, one whose atoms cancel scores near 0. The average is 0.73 on BACE and drops to 0.43 for six-atom BACE fragments, so on the larger fragments the signed convention discards most of the atom-level signal. Mixed-sign fragments are common rather than exceptional at 52% of 956 fragments. On PTR1 the effect is far weaker, at 0.90 and 47% of 102 fragments: its molecules carry 4.4 fragments against BACE’s 7.2, and smaller fragments hold fewer atoms to cancel each other out. The instability therefore scales with fragment size, and BACE exposes this, whereas PTR1 does not. Summing magnitudes avoids the cancellation and raises the baseline (0.399 to 0.426 on BACE), while normalizing by size removes the reward for large fragments and cuts it to 0.223. Across the four combinations the baseline covers 0.223–0.426 on BACE.

title: Improved Training of Strong Stochastic Flow Maps
prompt:
I’ve been sketching out a Wong–Zakai (WZ) Eulerian loss for flow matching on SDEs. The idea is to replace the Brownian path on [s,t] with its shifted Legendre approximation, giving the random ODE

\begin{equation}
    \label{eq:wz-rode-app}
    \dot\bX_r^{(N)} = \bv_r^{(N)}(\bX_r^{(N)}), \qquad \bv_r^{(N)}(\bx) \coloneq \bm b_r(\bx) + \nu_r \dot\bW_r^{(N,s,t)}, \qquad \bX_s^{(N)} = \bx,
\end{equation}

and denote its flow by \(\bm\Psi_{s,t}^{(N)}(\bx; \mathcal I_{s,t})\). Since \(\bW^{(N,s,t)}\) is a polynomial, the derivative is available in closed form. Because the noise is additive, the Itô and Stratonovich interpretations coincide, which simplifies the analysis.

With this convention the Wong–Zakai Eulerian and Lagrangian residuals are

\begin{align}
    \mathcal R_{\mathrm E}^{N,\theta} &\coloneq \mathfrak D_s \bm\Psi_{s,t}^\theta(\bx;\mathcal I_{s,t}) + \big(\nabla_\bx \bm\Psi_{s,t}^\theta(\bx;\mathcal I_{s,t})\big)\,\bv_s^{(N)}(\bx),
        \label{eq:wz-eulerian-residual}\\
    \mathcal R_{\mathrm L}^{N,\theta} &\coloneq \mathfrak D_t \bm\Psi_{s,t}^\theta(\bx;\mathcal I_{s,t}) - \bv_t^{(N)}\big(\bm\Psi_{s,t}^\theta(\bx;\mathcal I_{s,t})\big).
        \label{eq:wz-lagrangian-residual}
\end{align}

Equivalently, \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm E}^{N,\theta} = D_s^{(N)}\bm\Psi_{s,t}^\theta\), where \(D_s^{(N)} \coloneq \mathfrak D_s + \bv_s^{(N)}(\bx)^\top\nabla_\bx\) is the material derivative with \(\partial_s\) replaced by the fixed-path derivative and \(\bv_s\) by the Wong–Zakai field. In contrast to the Doss–Sussmann setting, the vector field \(\bv^{(N)}\) contains \(\nu_r\dot\bW_r^{(N,s,t)}\), which depends on all \(N\) coefficients; thus both residuals carry the full path information to the network.

My setup is the full strong error grid: \(\ex\|\bX_1 - \bX_1^\theta\|^2\) against a 512-step Euler–Maruyama reference on 1024 shared initial conditions and Brownian paths (eval seed 12345). All losses share the closed-form-increment map. My current baseline uses the Doss–Sussmann (DS) iMF Eulerian loss with N=4, and I get the following strong error values:

NFE=2: 1.11MSE

title: Improved Training of Strong Stochastic Flow Maps
prompt:
I've been developing an exponential lift for flow matching that gives a new parameterization of the flow map. The idea is to write the map as an exponentially weighted Euler–Maruyama step of the form

\begin{align}
    \bm\Psi_{s,t}^\theta(\bx;\mathcal I_{s,t}) = \frac{\alpha_s}{\alpha_t}\bx + 2\frac{\mathcal A_{s,t}}{\alpha_t} \bu_{s,t}^\theta(\bx;\mathcal I_{s,t}) + \frac{1}{\alpha_t} (\bW_{\langle \bm M^\alpha\rangle_t} - \bW_{\langle \bm M^\alpha\rangle_s}),
\end{align}

where \(\mathcal A_{s,t} \coloneq \int_s^t\rmd r\; \alpha_r\) and \(\bm M_t^\alpha \coloneq \int_{t_0}^t \rmd \bW_r\; \alpha_r\nu_r\) and \(\langle \bm M^\alpha \rangle_t\) is its quadratic variation. These quantities can be written in closed form for common choices of noise schedules. On the diagonal the drift of this parameterization is \(2\bu_{t,t}^\theta(\bx; \bm 0) - \frac{\dot\alpha_t}{\alpha_t}\bx\), which equals the teacher SDE drift if and only if \(\bu_{t,t}^\theta(\bx; \bm 0) = \bu_t^\theta(\bx)\); the decoupled architecture together with a \((t-s)\)-gated coefficient injection makes this exact at initialization. Moreover, the Itô integral itself is a martingale which is a time-changed Brownian motion, so we construct our Brownian approximation around this path, i.e., \(\mathcal I_{s,t}\) is built from \(\bW_{\langle \bm M^\alpha\rangle_t}\). This is important: if the coefficients of the approximation are constructed from the original Brownian path, then one must use numerical quadrature to approximate the Itô integral rather than computing it exactly as we can via our closed-form formulæ. This closed-form martingale also enables us to use an instantaneous drift matching loss, unlike regressing to a small Euler–Maruyama step.

My setup is as follows. I begin with the pre-trained DMF-XL/2+ checkpoint and add a small diffusion head to the original backbone. I do the whole parameterization with respect to the non-lifted SDE; this entry forms the most faithful replication of SSFM in the setting of fine-tuning from a pre-trained large deterministic model. I then add in the improvements in the following order: the exponential lift, the closed-form martingale of the Brownian path, and training via drift matching. For the first three rows of the ablation grid (SSFM, + exponential lift, + closed-form martingale) I instead use a single Euler–Maruyama step of size 0.01; the SSFM and exponential-lift variants additionally learn a randomly initialized diffusion head. I use the AdamW optimizer with \(\beta_1 = 0.9\), \(\beta_2 = 0.95\), \(\epsilon = 10^{-8}\), no weight decay, a learning rate of \(10^{-4}\), gradient clipping at 1.0, bf16-mixed precision, and an effective batch size of 128 (64 × 2 gradient accumulation). I train for 100k optimizer steps, evaluating at NFE ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} on ImageNet-256 with N=3.

My current baseline, the SSFM replication at 50k steps on ImageNet-256, gets the following numbers. At NFE=1: FID 197.11, FD_DINOv2 2116.9, ImageReward -2.214, PickScore 18.13, HPSv2.1 0.1506. At NFE=8: FID 11.09, FD_DINOv2 229.1, ImageReward -0.493, PickScore 19.78, HPSv2.1 0.2177. At NFE=16: FID 4.82, FD_DINOv2 135.6, ImageReward -0.312, PickScore 20.04, HPSv2.1 0.2253.

I've been iterating on a Feynman–Kac corrector (FKC) setup for sampling from annealed densities that are not the marginals of any single trained model, specifically targeting \(\pi_t \propto p_t^\beta\) or products of experts \(\pi_t \propto \prod_i (q_t^i)^{\beta_i}\). title: Investigating the Impact of Learner Errors on Social Bias in Large Language Models
prompt:
I've been iterating on a setup where learner errors are injected into prompts to see how they affect model behavior. The idea is to simulate L2 writing by introducing four error types simultaneously into the input, and my default configuration uses the gender category because gender is the only demographic axis shared across all three benchmarks I'm working with, which lets me compare trends across them. Since the four error types co-occur in real L2 writing, this setting makes the evaluation closer to a realistic scenario.

My setup uses five open-weight models from three families: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, Mistral-Small-3.2-24B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. I'm measuring accuracy on tasks whose correct answer is not tied to a stereotype, to rule out the objection that any accuracy loss merely reflects a general degradation of comprehension. Specifically, I'm using MMLU, which contains no demographic content, and the disambiguated split of BBQ, where the context states the correct answer. My baseline with clean prompts (0% error rate) gets the following: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on MMLU accuracy 68.8%, on BBQ disambiguated gender 95.7%, race 96.3%, religion 93.1%; Mistral-Small-3.2-24B-Instruct on MMLU accuracy 82.5%, on BBQ disambiguated gender 100.0%, race 99.6%, religion 98.8%; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on MMLU accuracy 75.2%, on BBQ disambiguated gender 98.6%, race 98.4%, religion 94.6%; Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct on MMLU accuracy 79.0%, on BBQ disambiguated gender 98.8%, race 97.7%, religion 97.0%; Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct on MMLU accuracy 82.8%, on BBQ disambiguated gender 100.0%, race 100.0%, religion 98.2%.

title: What the Author Wrote, What the Agent Reads: Silent Cue Loss in Enterprise Document Ingestion
prompt:
I've been brainstorming about how document parsing fidelity affects downstream retrieval of marked requirements from real policy documents. My setup is: all experiments use Claude Opus 4.6, temperature 0. Question generation and second-opinion judging use different model families, so no model both writes and answers a question. A policy document contains several requirement-like sentences; the author marked some (red text or highlight) and left others unmarked. I ask:

\begin{quote}
\itshape List every requirement in this document that the author has singled out for special attention or elevated priority.
\end{quote}

Ground truth is the marked set, taken directly from OOXML run properties---never from judgement. Scoring is set retrieval (precision, recall, F1) with a false-positive rate measured against real \emph{unmarked} requirements from the same document, so a system that lists everything is penalised. Matching is lexical and deterministic: \textbf{no LLM judge is involved}. A gold requirement counts as retrieved when a run of four consecutive opening content words appears in the answer. That rule is deliberately conservative, and I verified it does not depress the numbers: only \emph{one} of the 332 gold requirements has fewer than four content words and is therefore unmatchable by construction, giving every arm a recall ceiling of $0.997$, and no unmarked distractor is unmatchable at all. Relaxing the rule to a three-word run or 60\% content-word overlap would accept a further $4.8\%$ of unmatched pairs, but inspection shows most of those are the looser rule wrongly matching a \emph{different} requirement that shares boilerplate wording, so I keep the strict form. Construction requires at least one marked and at least three unmarked requirements per document, and rejects any document whose marked sentences are the only ones carrying urgency words. This yields \textbf{84 documents} (332 marked, 4{,}192 unmarked distractors); 76--79 are scored in a given run, as a document is used only when every arm produces a representation under the size cap, so comparisons stay paired.

Every arm receives the same question over the same document and differs only in how the document was parsed. I'm comparing my formatting-aware parsing against docling conversion. My current baseline with docling on the 76 real policy documents gets micro F1 of 0.15, precision of 0.196, and a false-positive rate of 0.043.

My question about this setup: after switching from docling (my baseline above) to ours (formatting-aware parsing), predict the resulting value for each: 76 real policy documents (marked-requirement retrieval) micro F1 (in F1); 76 real policy documents (marked-requirement retrieval) precision (in precision); 76 real policy documents (marked-requirement retrieval) FP rate (in rate).
asked: 76 real policy documents (marked-requirement retrieval) micro F1 (in F1)
76 real policy documents (marked-requirement retrieval) precision (in precision)
76 real policy documents (marked-requirement retrieval) FP rate (in rate)

I've been iterating on isolating the contribution of typed role tokens in my formatting-aware parsing approach. The novel component of this system is not preserving cues—docx2python does that—but attaching typed roles to them. Isolating that contribution requires comparing our representation against the same representation with the role tokens removed and every inline cue marker retained. My setup is the upper panel: all six arms, 76 documents, 3 repeats, 1,368 calls, paired per-document macro F1 against ours. The pre-registered confirmatory test of the typing claim runs once on 79 documents with 6 repeats (1,422 calls) and three arms only, so the correction family is two hypotheses. Both arms in H1 show the model identical inline cue markers over byte-identical content, differing only in whether a typed role token is attached. On the 76 real policy documents for marked-requirement set retrieval, my baseline with untyped markup gets micro F1 of 0.605, precision of 0.811 proportion, and a false positive rate of 0.01.

title: What the Author Wrote, What the Agent Reads: Silent Cue Loss in Enterprise Document Ingestion
prompt:
I've been developing the parser's highlight disambiguation rule on the real corpus of policy documents. The idea is to type highlights by presence rather than by hue. My initial rule typed only yellow and dark-yellow highlights as \textsc{warning}. The shipped rule types \emph{any} highlight as \textsc{warning} except \texttt{WHITE} and \texttt{NONE}, which render identically to unhighlighted text and are not marks at all; a \texttt{RED} highlight escalates to \textsc{critical\_warning} alongside red text. Hue is still preserved in the serialized output, so a reader that wants to distinguish yellow from cyan can. Roles attach at \emph{block} level while spans carry raw inline markers, and that separation is what makes the salience-versus-typing ablation possible. My baseline gets a share of author-marked paragraphs receiving a salience role of 79.1% for the initial hue-restricted rule (yellow/dark-yellow highlights only).

My question about this setup: after switching from initial hue-restricted rule (yellow/dark-yellow highlights only) (my baseline above) to shipped any-visible-hue rule (any highlight except WHITE/NONE as Warning; RED escalates to Critical_Warning), predict the resulting value for each: share of author-marked paragraphs receiving a salience role (real corpus of policy documents) percentage of paragraphs receiving a salience role (in %).

title: BatchBench: Benchmarking AI Robustness to Batch Effects and Domain Shift in Biomedical Images - A JUMP Cell Painting Leaderboard
prompt:
I’ve been thinking about domain-invariant training, specifically using an adversarial domain classifier (DANN). The idea is to encourage representations that do not depend on the domain during training, adversarially, using the source identifier as the domain label. My setup is a ResNet18 backbone whose first convolution takes five input channels. I train with standard empirical risk minimization on the training sources and apply the classifier to the test sources unchanged. My baseline gets: overall test set accuracy 0.175, POSCON subset accuracy 0.465, TARGET subset accuracy 0.012, REST subset accuracy 0.002.

My question about this setup: after switching from ResNet18 (no adaptation) (my baseline above) to DANN, predict the resulting value for each: Overall test set accuracy (in fraction); POSCON subset accuracy (in fraction); TARGET subset accuracy (in fraction); REST subset accuracy (in fraction).
